title: Adaptive Gating Sparsity Control for Efficient Long-Context Inference: Dynamic Threshold Learning in Gated Attention
description: Problem: While the anchor paper demonstrates that head-specific sigmoid gating after SDPA reduces attention sinks and improves long-context extrapolation, the gating scores are applied uniformly during inference without exploiting their inherent sparsity for computational savings. Dynamic sparsity patterns from learned gates could enable selective KV-cache pruning and sparse attention computation, but no principled mechanism exists to translate gating scores into inference-time efficiency gains. Proposed Method: We introduce Threshold-Adaptive Gated Attention (TAGA), which augments the sigmoid gate from the anchor paper with a learnable per-head sparsity threshold trained via a differentiable straight-through estimator. During inference, heads with gate magnitudes below their threshold skip KV-cache retrieval entirely, enabling dynamic KV-cache eviction and sparse attention computation. We additionally propose a token-level importance score derived from cumulative gate activations across layers to guide aggressive KV-cache compression without recomputation. Planned Experiments: (1) Train 1.7B and 7B dense models on 500B tokens comparing baseline softmax, anchor paper gated attention, and TAGA; (2) Evaluate perplexity on long-context benchmarks (SCROLLS, LongBench) at 8K–128K context lengths; (3) Measure wall-clock inference speedup and memory reduction at varying sparsity budgets (10%-70%); (4) Ablate threshold learning strategies and gate-derived eviction policies against static KV-cache pruning baselines like H2O and SnapKV.

title: Adaptive Gating Schedules for Attention Sinks: Dynamic Sparsity Control Across Training Stages and Context Lengths
description:
Problem: The anchor paper shows that post-SDPA sigmoid gating mitigates attention sinks and improves long-context extrapolation, but applies a static gating mechanism throughout training. We hypothesize that attention sink formation follows distinct phases during training, and that dynamically adapting gate behavior across training stages and context positions could yield superior performance compared to fixed gating.

Proposed Method: We introduce Adaptive Scheduled Gating (ASG), which modulates gate temperature and initialization as a function of training progress and token position. Specifically: (1) a curriculum-based gate temperature schedule that starts soft (near-uniform) and anneals to sharper sigmoid responses, allowing the model to first learn dense attention patterns then prune sinks; (2) position-aware gate biases initialized to discourage initial tokens from accumulating disproportionate attention mass; (3) a learnable per-layer gate threshold that balances sparsity versus expressiveness, regularized by an entropy penalty.

Experiments: We train 1.7B dense models on 500B tokens comparing static gating (anchor baseline), ASG variants, and ungated softmax. Evaluations include: perplexity on standard benchmarks, attention sink frequency analysis across layers/heads, RULER long-context benchmarks up to 128K tokens, and training stability metrics (gradient norms, loss spikes) across learning rates. Ablations isolate each ASG component's contribution.

title: Adaptive Gate Sparsity for Mixture-of-Experts Routing: Unifying Attention Sinks and Expert Load Imbalance
description: Problem: Large MoE language models suffer from two related pathological concentration phenomena: attention sinks (where specific tokens absorb disproportionate attention) and expert load imbalance (where few experts handle most tokens). The anchor paper shows head-specific sigmoid gating after SDPA mitigates attention sinks via query-dependent sparse gating scores. We hypothesize the same sparsity-inducing principle can be extended to MoE routing to simultaneously address both pathologies through a unified sparse gating framework. Method: We propose Sparse-Gated MoE (SG-MoE), which replaces standard softmax router scores with sigmoid-gated scores (as in the anchor's attention gating) applied to expert selection logits. This creates query-dependent sparse expert activation without auxiliary load-balancing losses. We further introduce a joint training objective coupling attention gate sparsity and routing gate sparsity to prevent correlated collapse. We additionally analyze whether attention-sink-free training generalizes to expert-sink-free routing. Experiments: (1) Train 1.7B dense and 7B MoE models on 500B tokens comparing standard softmax routing, top-k routing with auxiliary loss, and SG-MoE. (2) Measure expert utilization entropy, attention sink frequency, perplexity, and long-context benchmarks (SCROLLS, RULER). (3) Ablate sigmoid vs. softmax routing gates and joint vs. decoupled objectives. (4) Evaluate scaling behavior at 15B MoE.

title: Adaptive Gating Frequency Across Transformer Layers: When and Where Does Sigmoid Gating Matter Most?
description:
Problem: The anchor paper demonstrates that applying a head-specific sigmoid gate uniformly after SDPA consistently improves performance, but applies this gating to all attention heads in all layers equally. This raises an important question: is uniform gating optimal, or do different layers and heads benefit asymmetrically from gating? Early layers may develop syntactic representations while later layers handle semantic reasoning, suggesting heterogeneous gating needs.

Proposed Method: We propose Layer-Adaptive Gated Attention (LAGA), which learns to allocate gating capacity non-uniformly across layers and heads using a differentiable budget constraint. Specifically, we introduce per-layer gating probability parameters trained end-to-end with an L1 sparsity regularizer on gating activations, allowing the model to discover which layers/heads most benefit from non-linear gating. We additionally analyze attention sink distribution patterns across layers to understand the correlation between sink prevalence and gating utility.

Experiments: (1) Train 1.7B dense models with uniform vs. adaptive gating on 500B tokens, comparing perplexity and downstream benchmarks. (2) Visualize learned gating distributions across layers/heads to identify structural patterns. (3) Evaluate long-context extrapolation (4K→32K) to test whether adaptive gating better suppresses attention sinks in specific layers. (4) Ablate budget constraints to find optimal gating density. (5) Transfer learned gating masks to larger models to test generalization.

title: Adaptive Gate Sparsity for Efficient Long-Context Inference: Trading Attention Sink Elimination for KV Cache Compression
description:
Problem: While gated softmax attention mitigates attention sinks and improves long-context extrapolation, its inference efficiency implications—particularly for KV cache management—remain unexplored. Attention sinks are known to cause naive KV cache eviction strategies (e.g., H2O, StreamingLLM) to fail, as sink tokens must be retained. If sigmoid gating eliminates attention sinks, it may fundamentally change which tokens are safe to evict, enabling more aggressive KV cache compression without quality degradation.

Proposed Method: We integrate head-specific sigmoid gating into existing KV cache eviction frameworks. Since gated attention produces query-dependent sparse activation patterns without fixed sink tokens, we design a dynamic eviction policy that uses gate activation magnitudes as token importance scores. We further propose a gate-aware prefill compression strategy that skips KV materialization for tokens receiving near-zero gate activations across heads.

Experiments: (1) Compare KV cache compression ratios at iso-quality on LongBench, RULER, and Needle-in-Haystack between standard softmax + eviction baselines versus gated attention + gate-aware eviction. (2) Ablate gate thresholds and eviction schedules. (3) Profile wall-clock inference speedup and memory reduction on 7B and 70B models at 32K–128K context lengths. (4) Analyze correlation between gate sparsity patterns and optimal eviction decisions.

title: Adaptive Gating Schedules for Attention: From Sparse to Dense via Curriculum Learning
description:
Problem: The paper shows that head-specific sigmoid gating after SDPA improves performance by inducing sparsity and eliminating attention sinks. However, the gating mechanism is static throughout training — it neither adapts to the learning phase nor to the semantic complexity of different token contexts. We hypothesize that dynamically scheduling gating sparsity during training (curriculum over gating intensity) and allowing context-sensitive gate modulation could yield further gains, especially in reasoning-heavy and long-context tasks.

Proposed Method: We introduce Curriculum Gated Attention (CGA), which (1) starts training with dense gating (gates near 1, minimal sparsity) to allow early representation learning without constraint, then progressively anneals toward sparse gating regimes via a cosine schedule; and (2) augments the head-specific sigmoid gate with a lightweight MLP conditioned on a summarized context vector, enabling input-adaptive gating beyond per-head scalars.

Experiments: We train 1.7B dense models on 1T tokens, comparing static sigmoid gating (baseline from anchor paper), our curriculum schedule alone, context-adaptive gating alone, and the full CGA. Evaluations cover standard benchmarks (MMLU, HellaSwag), long-context extrapolation (RULER, LongBench), attention sink analysis, and training stability under varying learning rates. Ablations isolate curriculum scheduling from adaptive gating contributions.

title: Adaptive Gate Pruning: Leveraging Sparse Sigmoid Gates for Dynamic Attention Head Removal at Inference
description:
Problem: Large language models with multi-head attention suffer from computational redundancy at inference time. Many attention heads contribute minimally to outputs, yet standard pruning methods require expensive post-hoc analysis or retraining. The gated attention paper shows that head-specific sigmoid gates naturally produce sparse, query-dependent scores—we hypothesize these learned gate magnitudes directly encode head importance in an input-adaptive manner, enabling principled dynamic pruning without additional analysis.

Proposed Method: We augment gated softmax attention by adding a lightweight learned threshold per head, trained jointly with a sparsity-inducing regularizer (e.g., L0 or straight-through Gumbel). At inference, heads whose gate activations fall below a dynamic, context-sensitive threshold are entirely skipped. We further propose a gate-magnitude-based static pruning schedule derived from aggregate gate statistics on calibration data, providing a zero-overhead deployment option. The dual sparse gating from the anchor paper serves both model quality and as a natural pruning signal.

Experiments: (1) Train 1.7B dense gated-attention models with sparsity regularization at varying budgets; (2) Compare against magnitude, gradient, and Taylor-expansion pruning baselines; (3) Evaluate perplexity-vs-FLOPs trade-offs on standard LM benchmarks and long-context tasks (SCROLLS, RULER); (4) Measure attention-sink retention under pruning; (5) Profile wall-clock speedups on A100 GPUs using sparse kernel implementations.

title: Adaptive Gate Sparsity via Learned Thresholding: Connecting Gated Attention to Dynamic Token Pruning for Efficient Long-Context Inference
description: Problem: While the anchor paper demonstrates that head-specific sigmoid gating improves attention quality and mitigates attention sinks, the gating scores are computed but never exploited for computational savings during inference. Sparse gating scores naturally identify low-contribution attention heads per query, yet the framework still performs full SDPA computation before gating. We propose leveraging the predictability of gate sparsity patterns to enable dynamic head-level early-exit and KV-cache pruning during long-context inference. Method: We introduce a lightweight gate predictor—a small MLP operating on the query vector alone—that estimates sigmoid gate magnitudes before SDPA computation. Gates predicted below a learnable threshold trigger head skipping, avoiding the costly attention computation entirely. We additionally use gate scores to selectively evict KV-cache entries with persistently low gate activation across decoding steps, reducing memory pressure. The threshold is jointly learned during training via a differentiable relaxation with a sparsity regularization term targeting a configurable FLOP budget. Experiments: We train 1.7B dense models on 500B tokens across multiple sparsity budgets (20%, 40%, 60% head-skip rates), measuring perplexity, FLOP reduction, latency on 32K–128K context benchmarks (RULER, LongBench), and KV-cache memory usage. We compare against static head pruning, H2O, and SnapKV baselines, demonstrating that gate-informed dynamic pruning achieves better quality-efficiency tradeoffs than prior methods.

title: Adaptive Gate Annealing: Dynamic Sparsity Scheduling in Gated Attention for Curriculum-Aware Long-Context Training
description: Problem: While the anchor paper shows that head-specific sigmoid gating after SDPA mitigates attention sinks and improves long-context extrapolation, the gating behavior is static throughout training. We hypothesize that dynamically scheduling gate sparsity during training—starting dense (gate values near 1) and progressively annealing toward sparse configurations—could better align with curriculum learning principles, especially when sequences grow progressively longer during training. Proposed Method: We introduce Gate Sparsity Annealing (GSA), where gate initialization and a learnable temperature parameter are scheduled across training phases. Early training uses near-uniform gates to ensure stable gradient flow and broad attention coverage; later phases enforce increasingly sparse gates via temperature scaling to sharpen context selectivity. We additionally incorporate a sparsity regularization term whose coefficient increases with training step, explicitly encouraging the model to identify and suppress attention sinks progressively. Planned Experiments: (1) Compare GSA against static gated attention and vanilla softmax on 1.7B dense models trained with staged context length curricula (2K→8K→32K tokens); (2) Evaluate long-context benchmarks (RULER, LongBench) and standard NLP tasks; (3) Ablate annealing schedule shapes (linear, cosine, step); (4) Analyze attention sink emergence across training checkpoints using attention entropy metrics; (5) Test transfer to 7B models.

title: Adaptive Gate Calibration for Attention Sinks in Long-Context Retrieval: A Mechanistic Study
description: Problem: While the anchor paper shows that head-specific sigmoid gating after SDPA mitigates attention sinks and improves long-context extrapolation, it remains unclear how gating interacts with structured long-context tasks (multi-hop retrieval, needle-in-a-haystack, long-document QA) and whether gate magnitudes can be dynamically calibrated post-hoc without full retraining. Existing sink-mitigation strategies (attention bias, positional interpolation) are largely orthogonal to gating and their combination is unexplored. Proposed Method: We introduce GateCal, a lightweight post-training calibration procedure that fine-tunes only the sigmoid gate parameters (head-specific scale and bias) on a small curated corpus of long-context examples (∼50M tokens), freezing all other weights. We additionally propose a sink-aware gate regularization loss that penalizes excessive concentration of gate mass on early sink tokens, diagnosed via an entropy-based sink score. GateCal is applied to both a gated-attention pretrained model (from the anchor) and a vanilla softmax baseline to isolate gating's contribution. Experiments: (1) Perplexity and RULER benchmark across 4K–128K context lengths; (2) LongBench and HELMET suite for downstream long-context tasks; (3) Ablation of gate granularity (head-level vs. layer-level vs. query-dependent); (4) Efficiency analysis of calibration cost vs. full fine-tuning. Expected outcome: GateCal achieves 80% of full retraining gains at <1% compute, confirming gate parameters as a critical, low-dimensional bottleneck for long-context generalization.

title: Adaptive Gating Schedules for Attention: Dynamic Sparsity Control During Training and Inference
description:
Problem: The gated attention mechanism fixes the sigmoid gate's behavior uniformly across training, but optimal sparsity levels may vary across training phases, model depth, and input domains. Early training may benefit from denser attention for knowledge acquisition, while later stages and long-context inference may profit from sparser gating. Similarly, different layers (shallow vs. deep) and token types (content vs. positional) may require different sparsity regimes.

Proposed Method: We introduce Adaptive Gating Schedules (AGS) that dynamically modulate the sigmoid gate's temperature and bias parameters as a function of (1) training step (curriculum-based sparsity annealing), (2) layer depth (depth-adaptive gate initialization), and (3) input characteristics (content-aware gate calibration via a lightweight MLP predictor). The temperature controls the sharpness of the sigmoid, transitioning from soft near-uniform gating early in training to hard sparse gating later.

Experiments: We train 1.7B dense models on 500B tokens comparing fixed gates vs. AGS variants. We evaluate: (1) perplexity on standard benchmarks, (2) long-context extrapolation (4K→32K), (3) attention sink reduction metrics, (4) training stability via gradient norm tracking, and (5) few-shot task performance. Ablations isolate contributions of each scheduling component. We additionally probe whether curriculum sparsity enables training with even larger learning rates than static gated attention.

title: Adaptive Gating Sparsity for Efficient Long-Context Inference: Training-Free Calibration of Head-Specific Sigmoid Gates
description: Problem: While head-specific sigmoid gating after SDPA improves quality and mitigates attention sinks, it introduces uniform computational overhead across all heads and sequence positions during inference. In long-context settings, different attention heads specialize differently (local vs. global patterns), suggesting that gate activation sparsity could be exploited to skip unnecessary attention computations dynamically. Proposed Method: We propose GateSparse, a framework that (1) profiles the empirical gate activation distributions of pre-trained gated-attention models across heads and layers using a small calibration corpus, (2) learns head-specific threshold predictors that classify gates as near-zero (prunable) before computing full SDPA, and (3) integrates this with a speculative skipping mechanism where low-gate heads use cached or approximate attention outputs. The threshold predictors are lightweight MLPs taking query statistics as input, trained with a sparsity-accuracy Pareto objective. This requires no retraining of the base model. Experiments: We evaluate on (1) standard benchmarks (MMLU, HellaSwag) to verify accuracy retention, (2) long-context tasks (RULER, LongBench) at 32K-128K tokens measuring perplexity and task accuracy, (3) wall-clock inference speedup on A100s, and (4) ablations comparing fixed vs. adaptive thresholds and different calibration set sizes. We target 30-50% FLOPs reduction with <1% accuracy degradation.

title: Adaptive Gating Frequency Across Transformer Layers: When and Where Sigmoid Gates Matter Most
description: Problem: The anchor paper applies head-specific sigmoid gating uniformly after SDPA across all layers, but different layers in transformers are known to serve distinct roles (e.g., early layers capture syntactic patterns, middle layers semantic reasoning, later layers task-specific predictions). Applying identical gating uniformly may be suboptimal, and understanding which layers benefit most from gating remains unexplored. Proposed Method: We introduce Layer-Adaptive Gating (LAG), which learns a per-layer gating budget during training via differentiable binary concrete relaxations. Each layer independently determines whether to apply sigmoid gating, the gate granularity (head-specific vs. channel-specific), and gate strength via a learned scalar temperature. We also propose a structured pruning variant that freezes gating decisions post-training for inference efficiency. Planned Experiments: (1) Train 1B and 7B dense models on 500B tokens, comparing uniform gating vs. LAG on perplexity and downstream benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, LongBench). (2) Analyze which layer indices converge to active gates and correlate with attention entropy and attention sink metrics. (3) Evaluate long-context extrapolation (4K→32K) to test whether layer-selective gating better mitigates attention sinks than uniform gating. (4) Ablate gate granularities and temperature schedules to identify critical design choices.

title: Adaptive Gate Annealing: Dynamic Sparsity Schedules for Gated Attention During Pre-training
description: Problem: The anchor paper demonstrates that head-specific sigmoid gating after SDPA improves performance and mitigates attention sinks, but treats gating as a static mechanism throughout training. However, attention patterns evolve dramatically across training stages—early training requires dense attention to build coherent representations, while later stages benefit from sparse, focused attention. A fixed sigmoid gate may be suboptimal across this entire trajectory. Proposed Method: We introduce Adaptive Gate Annealing (AGA), where the sigmoid gate's temperature and bias are scheduled dynamically during pre-training. Specifically, we parameterize each head's gate as σ((h(x) - b(t))/τ(t)), where b(t) and τ(t) follow learnable-but-scheduled trajectories: starting with high temperature (near-uniform gating) and gradually annealing toward sparse, discriminative gating. We also explore curriculum-based schedules where annealing rate adapts to loss plateau detection. Experiments: We train 1.7B dense models on 500B tokens comparing (1) static sigmoid gating, (2) linear annealing, (3) cosine annealing, and (4) loss-adaptive annealing schedules. Evaluations include standard benchmarks, attention sink frequency across layers, long-context extrapolation (8k→32k), and training stability metrics. We additionally probe intermediate checkpoints to characterize how representation quality co-evolves with gate sparsity patterns.

title: Adaptive Gate Annealing: Dynamic Sparsity Scheduling in Gated Attention for Curriculum-Aware Long-Context Learning
description: Problem: While head-specific sigmoid gates after SDPA improve attention quality and mitigate attention sinks, the gates are trained with fixed objectives throughout training. We hypothesize that the sparsity profile induced by these gates should evolve during training—starting denser to capture broad contextual signals early, then becoming sparser to develop specialized head behaviors—analogous to curriculum learning. Proposed Method: We introduce Adaptive Gate Annealing (AGA), which augments gated attention with a learnable per-head temperature parameter applied to the sigmoid gate, scheduled via a curriculum that transitions from low-temperature (near-uniform, dense) to high-temperature (sparse, selective) gating over training. We also propose a sparsity regularization loss that encourages heads to specialize across semantic roles (local syntactic, long-range coreference, cross-document). The gate temperatures are jointly optimized with model parameters but with a slower learning rate schedule. Experiments: We train 1.7B dense transformer models on 200B tokens, comparing: (1) standard softmax, (2) fixed sigmoid gate (baseline from anchor), (3) AGA with cosine annealing, (4) AGA with data-difficulty-driven scheduling. Evaluation covers perplexity, long-context benchmarks (RULER, LongBench), attention sink metrics, and head specialization analysis via probing classifiers. We expect AGA to outperform fixed gating on contexts exceeding 32K tokens.

title: Adaptive Gating Frequency: Learning When to Gate Across Layers and Heads in Transformers
description:
Problem: The anchor paper applies a uniform sigmoid gate after SDPA across all heads and layers, but different layers and heads are known to serve distinct functional roles (e.g., induction heads, positional heads, semantic heads). Applying identical gating everywhere may be suboptimal—some heads may benefit from strong gating while others may be degraded by it. We lack principled methods to determine where gating provides the most benefit.

Proposed Method: We introduce Selective Gated Attention (SGA), which learns a per-layer, per-head binary or soft routing decision determining whether to apply the sigmoid gate. We parameterize this routing via a lightweight meta-network that takes as input layer index, head index, and training-step statistics (e.g., attention entropy, gradient norms). During training, we use a differentiable relaxation (Gumbel-sigmoid) to jointly optimize gate placement and model weights. A sparsity regularizer encourages minimal gating while maintaining performance.

Experiments: (1) Train 1.7B dense models with SGA vs. uniform gating vs. no gating on 500B tokens, comparing perplexity and downstream benchmarks. (2) Analyze which layers/heads receive gates and correlate with known head function taxonomies. (3) Evaluate attention-sink mitigation selectively. (4) Test long-context extrapolation on SCROLLS and RULER benchmarks. (5) Ablate routing mechanisms (meta-network vs. learned scalar per head vs. random).

title: Adaptive Gate Calibration for Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Mitigating Context Dilution via Sparse Attention Gating
description: Problem: In Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), LLMs frequently suffer from 'context dilution'—retrieved passages containing relevant information receive insufficient attention weight relative to irrelevant context or the query tokens, degrading answer quality. Standard softmax attention distributes probability mass broadly, and attention sinks further concentrate weights on uninformative tokens. The gated attention mechanism from the anchor paper mitigates attention sinks and introduces query-dependent sparsity, suggesting it could selectively amplify relevant retrieved content. Proposed Method: We extend head-specific sigmoid gating with a retrieval-awareness objective: during fine-tuning, we add a lightweight auxiliary loss that encourages gates corresponding to heads attending to gold-passage spans to maintain high activation, while suppressing gates on irrelevant context spans. This 'RAG-calibrated gating' requires only passage-level relevance labels (cheaply obtained from existing RAG datasets) and no architectural changes beyond the sigmoid gate. We further introduce a gate entropy regularizer to maintain sparsity without collapsing all gates. Experiments: We evaluate on KILT benchmarks (NQ, TriviaQA, HotpotQA), multi-hop reasoning (MuSiQue), and long-context RAG (SCROLLS) using 1.7B and 7B dense models. Ablations compare gate position, auxiliary loss weight, and entropy regularization strength, measuring EM/F1, faithfulness scores, and attention distribution entropy over retrieved vs. irrelevant spans.

title: Adaptive Gate Temperature Annealing for Gated Attention: Bridging Sparse and Dense Regimes During Training
description:
Problem: The sigmoid gate in gated attention introduces a fixed non-linearity that treats all training stages equally, yet optimal sparsity likely varies across training phases—early training may benefit from denser attention for rapid feature discovery, while later stages profit from sparse gating for specialization and reduced attention sink. How sparsity should evolve during training remains unexplored.

Proposed Method: We introduce Gated Attention with Temperature-Annealed Sparse Gates (GATES), where the sigmoid gate is parameterized as σ(x/τ(t)), with τ(t) a learnable or scheduled temperature that decreases from a high value (near-uniform/dense) to a low value (near-binary/sparse) over training. We additionally propose a head-specific learned annealing rate, allowing different attention heads to converge to different sparsity levels autonomously. A regularization loss encourages diversity in per-head final sparsity profiles.

Experiments: (1) Train 1.7B dense models on 300B tokens comparing fixed-gate baseline vs. fixed-schedule annealing vs. learned per-head annealing; (2) Measure attention sink formation dynamics throughout training as a function of gate temperature; (3) Evaluate long-context extrapolation (4K→32K) and perplexity on standard benchmarks; (4) Analyze emergent head specialization patterns via sparsity profiles; (5) Ablate annealing schedules (linear, cosine, exponential) to identify optimal curriculum.

title: Adaptive Gate Temperature Scheduling: Dynamic Sparsity Control in Gated Attention for Continual and Domain-Shifted Pretraining
description: Problem: The anchor paper demonstrates that head-specific sigmoid gating after SDPA improves LLM performance by inducing sparsity and mitigating attention sinks. However, the gating behavior is static throughout training—the same sigmoid nonlinearity applies regardless of training phase, domain shift, or data curriculum. We hypothesize that dynamically controlling gate sparsity during training could provide additional benefits: dense gates early in training for broad feature capture, transitioning to sparse gates later for specialization and efficiency. Method: We introduce a learnable per-head temperature parameter τ applied to the sigmoid gate (sigmoid(x/τ)), with τ initialized high (near-uniform) and annealed via a scheduled or meta-learned curriculum. We additionally explore domain-conditioned gating where τ adapts based on detected data domain (code, math, natural language), enabling domain-specific sparsity profiles within a single model. We implement this atop the anchor paper's best-performing gating variant and train 1.7B dense models on mixed-domain corpora with structured curricula. Experiments: (1) Compare fixed vs. annealed τ schedules on perplexity and downstream benchmarks; (2) Evaluate long-context extrapolation with domain-adaptive gates; (3) Analyze per-head sparsity trajectories and attention-sink suppression across domains; (4) Ablate meta-learned vs. hand-scheduled τ annealing strategies.

title: Adaptive Gate Annealing: Dynamic Sparsity Scheduling in Gated Attention for Curriculum-Aware Long-Context Learning
description: Problem: While the anchor paper demonstrates that head-specific sigmoid gating after SDPA mitigates attention sinks and improves long-context extrapolation, the gating mechanism is applied uniformly throughout training. We hypothesize that the optimal sparsity regime of these gates should evolve across training stages: dense early attention promotes broad pattern acquisition, while sparser gating later encourages specialization and efficient long-range focus. Method: We propose Adaptive Gate Annealing (AGA), a training curriculum that dynamically schedules the temperature and initialization bias of sigmoid gates across training phases. Specifically, we introduce a learnable per-head gate bias initialized to encourage near-uniform activation early in training, then apply a cosine annealing schedule that progressively shifts the bias toward sparser regimes. We additionally introduce a gate entropy regularization term that decays over training to softly enforce this curriculum without constraining individual head behavior. We also explore decoupling the annealing schedule between shallow and deep layers. Experiments: We train 1.7B dense models on 1T tokens with and without AGA, evaluating on standard LM benchmarks, attention sink diagnostics (max attention score concentration), long-context RULER benchmarks at 8K/32K/128K, and training loss curves. We ablate annealing schedules, regularization weights, and layer-wise decoupling to isolate each component's contribution.

title: Adaptive Gate Calibration for Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Mitigating Context Dilution via Sparse Gated Attention
description: Problem: In Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), LLMs frequently fail to attend properly to relevant retrieved passages due to attention dilution—query-relevant tokens compete with noisy retrieved chunks, degrading factual grounding. Standard softmax attention spreads probability mass indiscriminately, and even modern positional encodings do not resolve selective passage focus. The gated attention paper shows that head-specific sigmoid gates reduce attention sinks and improve context handling, suggesting a natural application to RAG where selective suppression of irrelevant context is critical. Proposed Method: We introduce RAG-GateAttn, which applies learned sigmoid gates conditioned jointly on (1) the query head activations and (2) a lightweight relevance score derived from the retrieval model's embedding similarity. The gate modulates SDPA outputs per head, allowing the model to dynamically suppress low-relevance retrieved segments without modifying the retrieval pipeline. We further investigate training a small auxiliary 'relevance gating network' that is fine-tuned on RAG-specific supervision signals (e.g., answer overlap with retrieved passages). Experiments: We train 1.7B dense models on a 100B token mixture including retrieval-augmented data, evaluating on PopQA, TriviaQA, HotpotQA, and SCROLLS. Ablations compare gate conditioning strategies, gating positions, and RAG-specific versus general pretraining. We measure faithfulness, exact match, and out-of-distribution retrieval robustness.

title: Adaptive Gating Schedules for Attention: Dynamic Sparsity Control During Training and Inference
description:
Problem: The gated attention paper shows that head-specific sigmoid gates consistently improve LLM performance by inducing sparsity and eliminating attention sinks. However, the optimal degree of sparsity likely varies across training stages (early vs. late), context lengths, and task types. Applying a fixed sigmoid gate may leave performance on the table by not adapting gate behavior to these varying conditions.

Proposed Method: We introduce Adaptive Schedule Gated Attention (ASGA), where gate temperature and bias parameters are dynamically scheduled rather than learned solely from data. Specifically: (1) During training, we anneal a temperature parameter controlling sigmoid sharpness from high (soft/dense) to low (sharp/sparse), mimicking curriculum learning toward sparsity. (2) At inference, we introduce task-conditioned gate scaling, where a lightweight router predicts per-layer gate multipliers based on input statistics (e.g., sequence length, entropy of token distribution). (3) We investigate whether different attention heads should have heterogeneous sparsity profiles via a differentiable budget constraint.

Experiments: We train 1.7B dense models on 500B tokens, comparing fixed sigmoid gates vs. ASGA across perplexity, long-context benchmarks (SCROLLS, RULER), attention sink metrics, and downstream tasks. Ablations isolate training schedule vs. inference adaptation contributions, with analysis of learned sparsity patterns per layer and head.

title: Adaptive Gate Sparsity for Efficient Long-Context Inference: Learning to Prune Attention Sinks Dynamically
description:
Problem: While gated attention mitigates attention sinks and improves long-context extrapolation, the computational overhead of maintaining full KV-caches remains a bottleneck at inference time. The head-specific sigmoid gate in gated attention naturally produces sparse outputs, but this sparsity is not explicitly exploited for KV-cache compression or token eviction during generation.

Proposed Method: We leverage the query-dependent sigmoid gate scores as a dynamic importance signal to guide KV-cache eviction in long-context inference. Specifically, we propose Sparse Gate-Guided Eviction (SGGE): during generation, gate activation magnitudes are accumulated per key-value token across heads, forming a salience score. Tokens falling below an adaptive threshold are evicted from the KV-cache. We further introduce a lightweight calibration mechanism that adjusts per-layer eviction rates based on observed gate entropy, preserving layers with high attention diversity while aggressively compressing redundant ones.

Experiments: (1) Compare SGGE against H2O, StreamingLLM, and SnapKV on LongBench, RULER, and Needle-in-a-Haystack benchmarks using pretrained gated-attention models at 1.7B and 15B scales. (2) Measure KV-cache memory reduction and throughput improvements. (3) Ablate gate-based versus attention-score-based eviction signals. (4) Evaluate whether SGGE further suppresses residual attention-sink tokens compared to vanilla gated attention.

title: Adaptive Gate Calibration for Continual Learning in LLMs: Leveraging Sparse Sigmoid Gates to Mitigate Catastrophic Forgetting
description: Problem: Large language models suffer from catastrophic forgetting during continual fine-tuning on new domains, as updating attention weights disrupts previously learned representations. Existing methods (EWC, LoRA, replay) add overhead or require task boundaries. The gated attention paper shows head-specific sigmoid gates produce sparse, query-dependent modulation that reduces attention sinks and improves stability—properties that may naturally protect consolidated knowledge. Proposed Method: We introduce Gate-Calibrated Continual Attention (GCCA), which freezes pre-trained SDPA weights and learns lightweight head-specific sigmoid gates (one scalar per head per task delta) during sequential fine-tuning. Rather than regularizing all parameters, we use the sparsity structure of sigmoid gates as a natural mask: heads with low gate activation on prior tasks are preferentially repurposed for new tasks, while high-activation heads are penalized from large shifts. We additionally employ a gate-guided importance score (analogous to Fisher information but computed over gate outputs) to selectively expand gate capacity for novel tasks. Experiments: We evaluate on (1) sequential domain adaptation (coding→math→instruction-following) using perplexity and downstream benchmarks, (2) long-context retention after continual fine-tuning, and (3) parameter efficiency vs. LoRA and O-LoRA baselines across 1.7B and 7B models, measuring forgetting, plasticity, and attention sink recurrence.

title: Adaptive Gate Calibration for Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Mitigating Context Dilution via Sparse Gating in Long-Document LLMs
description: Problem: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems suffer from 'context dilution' where relevant retrieved passages are overwhelmed by irrelevant content in long contexts, partly because standard softmax attention creates uniform attention sinks that fail to discriminate signal from noise across thousands of tokens. While the anchor paper shows head-specific sigmoid gating reduces attention sinks and improves long-context extrapolation, its implications for RAG-specific retrieval fidelity remain unexplored. Method: We propose RAG-GatedAttn, which extends head-specific sigmoid gating with a lightweight document-boundary-aware calibration mechanism. Specifically, we introduce learnable gate bias vectors conditioned on passage boundary tokens, allowing the sparse gating scores to differentially modulate attention outputs from retrieved versus non-retrieved context segments. We train 1.3B and 7B models from scratch with and without this modification on a mixture of pretraining and synthetic RAG tasks. Experiments: (1) Multi-hop QA benchmarks (MuSiQue, HotpotQA) with varying numbers of retrieved passages (1-20); (2) Long-context needle-in-haystack retrieval accuracy comparing baseline softmax, standard gated attention, and RAG-GatedAttn; (3) Ablations on gate calibration granularity; (4) Probing analysis measuring attention sink concentration at distractor versus relevant passage tokens; (5) Scaling from 4K to 128K context windows.

title: Adaptive Gating Schedules for Attention: Learning When to Sparsify Across Layers and Training Stages
description:
Problem: The anchor paper applies a uniform head-specific sigmoid gate after SDPA across all layers and training stages. However, different layers encode qualitatively different information (syntactic vs. semantic), and optimal sparsity likely varies both by layer depth and training phase. A static gating scheme may leave performance gains on the table.

Proposed Method: We introduce Layer-Stage Adaptive Gating (LSAG), where gate activation functions and sparsity targets are jointly learned as functions of (1) layer index and (2) training step via lightweight meta-networks. Specifically, a small MLP predicts per-layer gate temperature and bias from layer embeddings, updated via a auxiliary sparsity-regularized loss. During warmup, gates start near-dense and progressively sharpen, guided by a curriculum that tracks gradient norm stability. We also explore heterogeneous gating families per layer (sigmoid, ReLU, softplus) selected by differentiable architecture search.

Experiments: (1) Train 1.7B dense models on 500B tokens comparing static vs. LSAG gating; (2) Ablate layer-adaptive vs. stage-adaptive components; (3) Evaluate attention sink mitigation, long-context perplexity (128K), and downstream benchmarks (MMLU, HumanEval, SCROLLS); (4) Analyze learned per-layer sparsity patterns to interpret emergent specialization; (5) Transfer LSAG schedules across model scales (400M to 7B) to test universality.

title: Adaptive Gate Pruning for Efficient Inference: Exploiting Sparsity Patterns in Gated Attention at Deployment Time
description: Problem: While gated attention improves LLM performance by inducing sparse gating scores in SDPA outputs, this sparsity remains largely unexploited during inference—computations are still performed for near-zero gated heads, wasting FLOPs. We propose leveraging the predictable, query-dependent sparsity structure revealed in gated attention to enable dynamic head-level computation skipping at inference time. Method: We analyze the distribution of sigmoid gate activations across heads, layers, and token types in pretrained gated attention models (both dense 1.7B and MoE 15B variants). We then train a lightweight 'gate predictor'—a small MLP operating on query representations—that forecasts which heads will produce near-zero gate values before executing SDPA, enabling early-exit head computation. We further investigate whether gate sparsity correlates with specific token roles (e.g., sink tokens, content tokens) to enable structured pruning schedules. Experiments: (1) Measure realized sparsity vs. accuracy tradeoffs on standard benchmarks (MMLU, HellaSwag, MATH); (2) Compare wall-clock speedup vs. baseline gated attention on A100/H100 hardware with custom CUDA kernels; (3) Evaluate long-context tasks (RULER, Needle-in-Haystack) to confirm sparsity-based skipping preserves the attention-sink mitigation benefits; (4) Ablate predictor architectures and training objectives including distillation from gate values.

title: Adaptive Gate Pruning for Efficient Inference: Exploiting Sparsity in Gated Attention at Deployment Time
description: Problem: While gated attention improves LLM quality and mitigates attention sinks, the sigmoid gate introduces per-head sparsity in SDPA outputs that remains unexploited during inference—every head still computes full attention despite many gates being near-zero. This wastes compute, especially for long contexts where attention is already expensive. Proposed Method: We develop a framework called GateSkip that dynamically prunes attention head computation at inference time by predicting gate magnitudes before full SDPA computation. Specifically, we train lightweight per-layer gate predictors (small linear probes on query/key projections) that estimate whether each head's sigmoid gate will fall below a learned threshold, skipping SDPA for those heads entirely and substituting zero or a cached approximation. We further propose a gate-aware KV-cache eviction policy: heads with consistently low gates across tokens can have their KV entries pruned more aggressively. Finally, we introduce a gate-regularized fine-tuning objective that encourages bimodal gate distributions, amplifying natural sparsity. Experiments: We evaluate on pretrained gated-attention models (released by the anchor paper) across latency benchmarks (prefill and decode throughput), accuracy benchmarks (MMLU, LongBench, RULER for long-context), and KV-cache memory reduction, comparing against standard attention, static head pruning, and speculative attention baselines across 1.7B and 15B model scales.

title: Adaptive Gate Pruning for Efficient Inference: Exploiting Sparsity in Gated Attention at Deployment Time
description: Problem: Gated attention improves LLM quality by introducing query-dependent sparse gating scores, but the computational overhead of computing and applying these gates at inference time offsets some efficiency gains. The emergent sparsity in gate activations represents an untapped opportunity for dynamic computation reduction. Proposed Method: We propose GatePrune, a framework that (1) profiles the distribution of sigmoid gate activations across heads and layers during calibration, (2) learns per-head threshold predictors that anticipate near-zero gates from query representations before computing full SDPA, and (3) applies structured head-skipping at inference time when predicted gates fall below learned thresholds. We additionally introduce a sparsity-aware fine-tuning stage using straight-through estimators to recover accuracy lost from hard thresholding. The method requires no architectural changes to the trained gated attention model. Experiments: We evaluate on the released gated attention MoE (15B) and dense (1.7B) models, measuring perplexity on standard benchmarks (WikiText-103, C4), downstream task accuracy (MMLU, HellaSwag, GSM8K), and wall-clock inference speedup on A100/H100 GPUs. We compare against magnitude-based head pruning and attention early-exit baselines. We also analyze whether gate-sparse heads correlate with attention-sink heads, providing mechanistic insight into the sparsity-sink connection.

title: Adaptive Gating Sparsity Control for Dynamic Context Length Generalization in Transformer LLMs
description: Problem: While the anchor paper shows that head-specific sigmoid gating after SDPA mitigates attention sinks and improves long-context extrapolation, the gate activation threshold remains fixed during inference. This limits adaptability: short-context inputs may benefit from denser attention patterns while very long contexts require sparser gating to maintain coherence and suppress sink tokens effectively. A principled mechanism to dynamically modulate gating sparsity as a function of sequence length remains unexplored. Proposed Method: We introduce Context-Adaptive Gated Attention (CAGA), which augments the head-specific sigmoid gate with a lightweight learned sparsity controller—a small MLP that takes as input the current sequence length embedding and per-head gate statistics (mean, variance) from recent tokens, outputting a per-head temperature parameter that rescales sigmoid logits. This induces softer gates for short sequences and sharper (sparser) gates for long sequences without retraining. We further propose a differentiable sparsity regularization loss encouraging monotonic sparsity increase with sequence length. Experiments: (1) Train 1.7B dense models on 3.5T tokens comparing CAGA vs. fixed gating baseline; (2) Evaluate perplexity at 2K, 8K, 32K, 128K context lengths; (3) Measure attention sink suppression via sink token concentration metrics; (4) Ablate temperature controller architectures and sparsity regularization strengths; (5) Test zero-shot generalization to context lengths beyond training distribution.

title: Adaptive Gate Calibration for Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Mitigating Context Dilution via Sparse Attention Gating
description: Problem: In Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), LLMs often fail to properly attend to retrieved passages when context windows are long, a phenomenon called 'context dilution.' Attention sinks and uniform attention distribution across irrelevant tokens degrade grounding in retrieved evidence. The anchor paper shows that head-specific sigmoid gates after SDPA reduce attention sinks and improve long-context extrapolation—properties directly relevant to RAG settings. Proposed Method: We introduce Retrieval-Aware Gated Attention (RAGA), which extends the head-specific sigmoid gate with a lightweight relevance-conditioned modulation signal. Specifically, we prepend a learned [RETRIEVAL] token to each retrieved passage chunk; its hidden state is projected into a per-head gate bias added to the sigmoid gate, biasing attention heads toward retrieved content without modifying the softmax kernel. During fine-tuning, we train only the gate projection layers on RAG-specific datasets, keeping base weights frozen. This allows efficient adaptation of pretrained gated-attention models. Experiments: We evaluate on PopQA, TriviaQA, HotpotQA, and ASQA benchmarks using pretrained gated-attention checkpoints released by the anchor paper. Ablations compare: (1) baseline softmax attention, (2) ungated sigmoid gate, (3) RAGA with relevance conditioning. We measure EM/F1, faithfulness scores, and attention entropy over retrieved vs. non-retrieved tokens to quantify context dilution reduction.

title: Adaptive Gate Calibration for Efficient KV Cache Compression in Long-Context LLMs
description:
Problem: Large language models struggle with efficient long-context inference because KV cache grows linearly with sequence length, forcing expensive eviction heuristics that often discard tokens the model still needs. Existing eviction methods (H2O, SnapKV) rely on cumulative attention scores to identify 'heavy hitters,' but attention sinks artificially inflate scores for early tokens, corrupting importance estimates.

Proposed Method: Leveraging the finding from Gated Attention that head-specific sigmoid gates suppress attention sinks and produce sparser, query-dependent attention distributions, we propose using the gate activations themselves as real-time KV cache importance signals. Specifically, we train lightweight gate-calibrated eviction heads: during inference, the sigmoid gate magnitude for each key position is accumulated across layers and used to rank and prune the KV cache dynamically. We further propose a gate-guided prefill compression step that merges low-gate tokens into summary vectors before caching, reducing memory footprint without full recomputation.

Experiments: (1) Perplexity on PG19 and SCROLLS at 32k–128k context lengths under varying cache budgets; (2) LongBench and RULER benchmarks comparing against H2O, SnapKV, and full-cache baselines; (3) Ablations on gate threshold sensitivity, layer-wise vs. uniform eviction, and transfer to models without native gating via post-hoc gate insertion. We target 50% KV cache reduction with <1% performance degradation.

title: Adaptive Gate Sparsity Scheduling: Dynamic Sigmoid Thresholding for Efficient Long-Context Inference
description: Problem: While gated attention with head-specific sigmoid gates improves performance and mitigates attention sinks, the gating mechanism applies uniform sigmoid thresholding across all layers, heads, and sequence positions during inference. This ignores the heterogeneous importance of attention patterns at different depths and positions, leaving potential efficiency gains unexploited—especially for long-context inference where KV-cache costs dominate. Proposed Method: We introduce Adaptive Gate Sparsity Scheduling (AGSS), which learns layer-wise and head-wise sparsity targets for the sigmoid gate during training using a differentiable sparsity regularization loss. At inference time, we exploit the resulting sparse gating scores to perform speculative KV-cache eviction: tokens whose gated attention output falls below a learned head-specific threshold are evicted from the cache in subsequent layers. We further propose a position-aware gate calibration that adjusts thresholds based on relative position to preserve performance on recent and landmark tokens. Experiments: (1) Train 1.7B dense models comparing fixed vs. adaptive gating on standard benchmarks (MMLU, HellaSwag, GSM8K); (2) Evaluate long-context performance on RULER and LongBench at 32K-128K context lengths; (3) Measure KV-cache memory reduction and throughput improvements versus full-cache and H2O baselines; (4) Ablate sparsity scheduling strategies across layers and heads.

title: Adaptive Gate Sparsity Scheduling: Curriculum-Based Gating Intensity for Efficient Long-Context LLM Training
description: Problem: The anchor paper shows that head-specific sigmoid gating after SDPA mitigates attention sinks and improves long-context extrapolation. However, it treats gate intensity as a fixed architectural choice throughout training. We hypothesize that the optimal sparsity level of the sigmoid gate should evolve during training—early stages benefit from denser attention for rapid knowledge acquisition, while later stages benefit from sparser gating for specialization and long-context generalization. Proposed Method: We introduce Adaptive Gate Sparsity Scheduling (AGSS), which parameterizes the sigmoid gate with a learnable temperature parameter β(t) that follows a curriculum schedule. We augment the gate as σ(β(t)·h_q) where β(t) increases monotonically (e.g., cosine or linear warmup) over training steps, progressively sharpening gate sparsity. We additionally propose a per-head sparsity regularization loss that encourages diversity in gating patterns across heads, preventing collapse. Planned Experiments: (1) Train 1.7B dense models on a 500B token subset comparing fixed vs. scheduled gating using the anchor paper's evaluation suite; (2) Evaluate perplexity scaling with context length (2K–128K tokens) using RULER and LongBench; (3) Ablate scheduling functions (linear, cosine, step) and regularization strengths; (4) Analyze attention sink frequency and gate activation distributions across training checkpoints to validate the curriculum hypothesis.

title: Adaptive Gate Calibration for Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Reducing Attention Sink in Long-Context Document Grounding
description:
Problem: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems struggle when relevant passages are buried in long retrieved contexts, partly because attention sinks cause models to over-attend to early tokens (e.g., BOS or initial document headers) rather than semantically critical spans. The gated attention paper shows sigmoid gating post-SDPA mitigates attention sinks and improves long-context extrapolation, but its RAG implications are unexplored.

Proposed Method: We introduce Retrieval-Aware Gate Calibration (RAGC), which augments the head-specific sigmoid gate with a lightweight, trainable passage-boundary signal. Specifically, we inject soft positional markers at retrieved document boundaries and condition the gate's bias term on local passage relevance scores (from a small retriever). This encourages gates to suppress sink formation at document delimiters rather than propagating irrelevant early-context attention. We fine-tune only the gate parameters on top of a frozen gated-attention LLM, keeping compute overhead minimal.

Experiments: (1) Long-context QA benchmarks (NaturalQuestions, HotpotQA, SCROLLS) with 16–128K context windows; (2) Attention sink visualization comparing baseline, vanilla gated attention, and RAGC; (3) Ablation over gate conditioning signals (boundary-only vs. relevance-weighted); (4) Scaling analysis across 1.7B and 7B model sizes; (5) Faithfulness metrics measuring grounding accuracy vs. parametric knowledge reliance.

title: Adaptive Gate Sparsity Scheduling: Dynamic Control of Attention Sink Suppression During Training
description: Problem: The anchor paper shows that sigmoid gating after SDPA mitigates attention sinks and improves long-context extrapolation, but applies a fixed gating mechanism throughout training. Attention sinks emerge gradually during training, suggesting that static gating may be suboptimal—early training may benefit from denser attention patterns for stable gradient flow, while later stages benefit from sparse gating to suppress sinks and improve generalization. Proposed Method: We introduce Adaptive Gate Sparsity Scheduling (AGSS), which dynamically adjusts the sparsity of head-specific sigmoid gates throughout training via a curriculum. Specifically, we parameterize gate temperature as a function of training step, beginning with near-uniform (dense) gating and progressively sharpening toward sparse binary-like gating. We additionally introduce an auxiliary loss that monitors attention entropy across heads, using it as a signal to modulate the sparsity schedule automatically rather than relying on fixed annealing. Planned Experiments: (1) Train 1.7B dense models on 300B tokens comparing static gates vs. AGSS across multiple sparsity schedules; (2) Measure perplexity, attention sink formation dynamics (per-layer entropy curves), and long-context needle-in-haystack retrieval at 8K–128K context; (3) Ablate temperature schedule shapes (linear, cosine, entropy-triggered); (4) Evaluate training stability under large learning rates as in the anchor paper.

title: Adaptive Gating Schedules for Attention: Learning When Sparsity Matters During Training
description:
Problem: The anchor paper demonstrates that a fixed sigmoid gate after SDPA consistently improves LLM performance by inducing sparsity and eliminating attention sinks. However, it applies gating uniformly throughout training without considering whether the optimal gating strength varies across training stages, model depth, or sequence positions. We hypothesize that early training benefits from denser attention to establish representational structure, while later training benefits from aggressive sparsification for generalization and long-context extrapolation.

Proposed Method: We introduce Curriculum Gated Attention (CGA), where gate initialization and regularization are scheduled dynamically during training. Specifically: (1) a temperature-annealed sigmoid gate that transitions from near-linear (dense) to sharp (sparse) behavior over training; (2) layer-wise adaptive gating where deeper layers receive stronger sparsity pressure via a depth-scaled regularization term; (3) a lightweight meta-controller that monitors per-head attention entropy and adjusts gate bias accordingly.

Experiments: We train 1.7B dense models on 500B tokens comparing fixed gates (baseline from anchor), our CGA variants, and no-gate baselines. Evaluations include: standard language modeling benchmarks, long-context tasks (SCROLLS, RULER), attention sink metrics across layers, training loss curves at different learning rates, and ablations of each CGA component. We aim to show adaptive gating schedules yield further improvements beyond static gating.

title: Adaptive Gating Schedules for Attention: Learning When to Be Sparse During Training
description: Problem: The anchor paper shows that head-specific sigmoid gates after SDPA improve performance and mitigate attention sinks, but applies a fixed gating mechanism throughout training. We hypothesize that the optimal gating intensity should evolve during training—early stages may benefit from denser, less sparse attention to build broad representations, while later stages profit from sparser, more focused attention for specialization. Method: We propose Curriculum Gated Attention (CGA), where the sigmoid gate includes a learnable temperature parameter per head that is annealed according to a schedule (or learned via meta-gradient), transitioning from near-linear (temperature→∞, gate≈0.5) to sharp sigmoid behavior (temperature→1) over training. We additionally introduce a sparsity regularization loss that activates progressively, encouraging heads to commit to sparse or dense roles. We compare against fixed gating, no gating, and hand-tuned temperature baselines. Experiments: Train 1.7B dense models on 300B tokens (subset of training regime from anchor), measuring (1) perplexity curves, (2) attention sink formation over training steps, (3) long-context extrapolation (8k→32k), and (4) head specialization via entropy analysis. Ablations cover annealing schedule shape (linear, cosine, step), regularization weight, and whether temperature should be per-head vs. per-layer.

title: Adaptive Gating Frequency: Learning When to Gate Across Transformer Layers for Efficient Long-Context Reasoning
description:
Problem: The anchor paper applies a uniform sigmoid gate after SDPA across all attention heads and layers. However, not all layers contribute equally to attention sink formation or long-context extrapolation—early layers may benefit more from sparse gating while later layers require dense attention patterns for complex reasoning. Applying gates uniformly may waste capacity or introduce unnecessary sparsity where dense attention is needed.

Proposed Method: We introduce Layer-Adaptive Gating (LAG), a learned binary or continuous mask over whether each transformer layer applies the head-specific sigmoid gate. We parameterize gating decisions using a lightweight meta-controller (a small MLP) conditioned on layer depth, head index, and sequence length statistics. During training, we use straight-through estimators or Gumbel-softmax relaxations to jointly optimize gate presence decisions alongside model weights. This produces a heterogeneous gating schedule—dense in some layers, sparse in others—discovered automatically.

Experiments: (1) Train 1.7B dense models with LAG vs. uniform gating on 500B tokens, measuring perplexity and long-context benchmarks (RULER, Needle-in-Haystack). (2) Analyze which layers learn to gate, correlating with attention entropy and sink formation. (3) Ablate meta-controller designs and training signals. (4) Test zero-shot transfer of discovered gating schedules to larger models (7B). We hypothesize LAG achieves better perplexity-compute tradeoffs than uniform gating.

title: Adaptive Gate Calibration for Continual Learning: Leveraging Sparse Attention Gates to Mitigate Catastrophic Forgetting in LLMs
description: Problem: Catastrophic forgetting remains a critical challenge when fine-tuning LLMs on sequential tasks. Existing approaches (LoRA, EWC, replay) don't exploit architectural properties of attention mechanisms that naturally identify task-relevant computation. The gated attention paper shows that head-specific sigmoid gates produce sparse, query-dependent outputs that suppress irrelevant heads—suggesting gates may encode task-specific attention patterns worth preserving during continual learning. Method: We propose GateCL, which monitors the sparsity patterns of sigmoid attention gates across tasks and uses gate activation statistics to (1) identify task-critical heads whose gates fire densely on task-specific inputs, (2) selectively freeze or apply differential learning rates to these heads during subsequent fine-tuning, and (3) store compact gate-activation 'signatures' per task as cheap replay anchors (instead of full exemplars). A lightweight gate-distillation loss encourages new tasks to preserve previous tasks' gate signatures on held-out probe inputs. Experiments: We evaluate on standard continual learning benchmarks (Split-SQUAD, SuperGLUE sequential, instruction-following streams), comparing against EWC, O-LoRA, and replay baselines. Ablations test: gate freezing vs. weight freezing, signature compression ratios, and whether the anti-attention-sink property of gated attention inherently reduces task interference across context lengths up to 32k tokens.

title: Adaptive Gate Calibration for Efficient KV Cache Compression in Long-Context LLMs
description:
Problem: Large language models struggle with efficient long-context processing due to quadratic KV cache memory growth. Existing KV cache eviction strategies rely on attention score heuristics (e.g., H2O, StreamingLLM) that are brittle and sensitive to attention sinks — artifacts that gated attention demonstrably mitigates. This creates an opportunity: if head-specific sigmoid gates eliminate attention sinks and produce sparser, more meaningful attention distributions, can we leverage gate activation magnitudes as superior signals for KV cache token importance scoring?

Proposed Method: We integrate head-specific sigmoid gates from gated softmax attention into a token retention policy for KV cache compression. Gate activation values across heads are aggregated into a per-token importance score, replacing raw attention weights in eviction decisions. We further propose a lightweight calibration module that dynamically adjusts eviction thresholds per head based on gate sparsity statistics observed during inference prefill.

Experiments: (1) Evaluate perplexity on PG-19, SCROLLS, and RULER long-context benchmarks at 8K-128K sequence lengths. (2) Compare against H2O, SnapKV, and PyramidKV baselines under matched memory budgets. (3) Ablate gate vs. attention-score signals for eviction. (4) Measure wall-clock throughput on A100 GPUs. We train 1.7B dense models on 500B tokens to ensure clean comparisons.

title: Adaptive Gating Sparsity for Efficient Long-Context Inference: Connecting Attention Gates to KV Cache Compression
description: Problem: Large language models with gated attention show improved long-context extrapolation, but inference efficiency at long contexts remains a bottleneck due to quadratic KV cache growth. The sparse gating scores produced by head-specific sigmoid gates (as identified in the anchor paper) represent an underexplored signal for runtime KV cache management—tokens that receive near-zero gate activations across multiple heads are candidates for eviction without quality loss. Method: We propose Gate-Guided KV Eviction (GGKVE), which monitors the sigmoid gate output magnitudes per token across attention heads during generation. Tokens whose cumulative gate-weighted attention falls below an adaptive threshold are evicted from the KV cache. We additionally train a lightweight predictor that anticipates gate sparsity patterns from early layers to enable proactive eviction before full forward passes. Unlike prior KV eviction methods (H2O, ScissorHands) that rely on attention scores alone, GGKVE leverages the richer non-linear gate signal that the anchor work shows is distinct from raw attention weights. Experiments: We evaluate on LongBench, RULER (128k context), and Needle-in-a-Haystack benchmarks using the released gated-attention models, measuring perplexity, downstream task accuracy, KV cache memory reduction (targeting 50-70%), and throughput on A100s, with ablations comparing gate-based vs. attention-score-based eviction strategies.

title: Adaptive Gating Schedules for Attention: Curriculum-Based Sparsity Induction During LLM Pretraining
description:
Problem: While head-specific sigmoid gating after SDPA demonstrably improves LLM performance, current approaches apply fixed gating architectures uniformly throughout training. It remains unknown whether the timing and degree of sparsity induction via gating matters—specifically, whether gradually introducing gating sparsity during training (analogous to curriculum learning) yields better representations than static gating from initialization.

Proposed Method: We introduce Curriculum Gated Attention (CGA), where the sigmoid gate's bias initialization and temperature are scheduled across training. Early training uses near-linear (warm) gates (high temperature, bias→+∞) mimicking standard softmax attention, progressively cooling toward sparse binary-like gating. We also explore layer-wise schedules where lower layers retain dense attention longer while upper layers sparsify earlier, motivated by the hierarchical feature hypothesis. The schedule parameters are either hand-designed or learned via a small meta-gradient controller.

Experiments: (1) Train 1.7B dense models on 200B tokens comparing static vs. curriculum gating across 5 schedule shapes (linear, cosine, step, layer-wise). (2) Evaluate perplexity, attention sink metrics, and long-context extrapolation (32K→128K). (3) Ablate gate temperature annealing vs. bias scheduling independently. (4) Test transfer: does curriculum-pretrained gating generalize better under continued pretraining on domain-specific corpora? We hypothesize curriculum gating reduces representation collapse in early layers and improves downstream task performance by 1-3% over static gating baselines.

title: Adaptive Gate Sparsity for Efficient Long-Context Inference: Trading Attention Sink Suppression for KV Cache Compression
description: Problem: While gated attention mitigates attention sinks and improves long-context extrapolation, the head-specific sigmoid gate introduces additional compute and does not directly reduce KV cache memory during inference—a critical bottleneck for long-context deployment. We hypothesize that the sparse gating scores learned by gated attention naturally identify which tokens are informationally redundant (previously masked by attention sinks), making them ideal signals for dynamic KV cache eviction. Proposed Method: We extend the post-SDPA sigmoid gate into a dual-purpose module: (1) during training, it retains its role as a sparsity-inducing non-linearity, and (2) during inference, the gate activation magnitudes serve as learned token importance scores for online KV cache pruning. We introduce a differentiable top-k eviction schedule trained end-to-end, allowing the gate to learn to produce high-magnitude scores for truly important tokens. A lightweight predictor uses gate statistics from early layers to preemptively evict tokens in deeper layers. Experiments: We evaluate on 1B–7B models trained from scratch and fine-tuned checkpoints from the anchor paper, testing on RULER, LongBench, and Needle-in-Haystack benchmarks at context lengths 8K–512K, comparing perplexity-memory tradeoffs against H2O, SnapKV, and StreamingLLM baselines.

title: Adaptive Gate Calibration for Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Suppressing Distractor Tokens via Sparse Sigmoid Gating
description:
Problem: In Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), LLMs must identify relevant passages among distractors. Standard softmax attention spreads probability mass broadly, making it hard to suppress irrelevant retrieved context—a phenomenon worsened by attention sinks forming on distractor tokens. The gated attention findings suggest sparse sigmoid gates can selectively suppress unimportant heads, motivating their targeted application in RAG settings.

Proposed Method: We augment a base LLM (e.g., Qwen-2.5 7B) with head-specific sigmoid gates after SDPA (as in the anchor paper) and introduce a RAG-specific auxiliary loss during fine-tuning that penalizes gate activations corresponding to distractor document tokens identified via annotated relevance labels. Additionally, we propose 'context-adaptive gate scaling,' where gate magnitudes are dynamically rescaled based on the ratio of retrieved document length to query length, preventing attention sink formation on padding/distractor tokens.

Experiments: (1) Evaluate on multi-document QA benchmarks (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, FRAMES) measuring exact match and distractor robustness. (2) Ablate: no gating vs. standard gating vs. RAG-calibrated gating. (3) Analyze gate sparsity patterns on relevant vs. distractor passages via attention visualization. (4) Test long-context RAG (32k+ tokens) where attention sink suppression matters most. (5) Compare against RAG-specific baselines like RECOMP and selective context compression.

title: Adaptive Gate Calibration for Mixture-of-Experts Routing: Coupling Head-Level Sparsity with Expert Selection
description:
Problem: In MoE-based LLMs, attention head gating (as shown in the anchor paper) and expert routing are currently independent mechanisms, despite both performing input-dependent sparse selection. This independence may create redundant or conflicting sparsity patterns that limit model capacity and training efficiency.

Proposed Method: We propose GateMoE, a joint gating framework that shares information between sigmoid attention gates and MoE router scores. Specifically, we aggregate head-gate activation statistics per token to produce a 'gate signature' vector, which is concatenated with the router's hidden state input to condition expert selection. Conversely, the selected expert identity is fed back as a learned bias to head-specific gate thresholds. This creates a bidirectional coupling where attention sparsity informs routing and vice versa. We further introduce a gate-router consistency regularization loss that encourages correlated sparsity patterns, reducing redundant computation.

Experiments: (1) Train 1.7B dense and 15B MoE models on 500B tokens comparing baseline gated attention, standard MoE, and GateMoE; (2) Measure perplexity, expert load balance, and attention sink prevalence; (3) Evaluate long-context extrapolation on SCROLLS and RULER benchmarks; (4) Analyze gate-router correlation matrices to verify coupled sparsity; (5) Ablate coupling direction (unidirectional vs. bidirectional) and regularization strength.

title: Adaptive Gate Sparsity Scheduling: Dynamic Thresholding of Sigmoid-Gated Attention for Curriculum-Aware Long-Context Learning
description: Problem: While the anchor paper demonstrates that head-specific sigmoid gating after SDPA mitigates attention sinks and improves long-context extrapolation, the gating mechanism applies a fixed learned threshold throughout training. We hypothesize that dynamically scheduling the sparsity level of sigmoid gates during training—starting dense (low sparsity) to capture broad context dependencies early, then progressively increasing sparsity—could further improve both convergence speed and long-context generalization. Method: We introduce a curriculum-based gate sparsity scheduler that modulates a learned per-head temperature parameter τ_h(t) controlling sigmoid sharpness, interpolating from near-linear (τ→0) to near-binary (τ→∞) gating over training. We additionally incorporate a differentiable top-k relaxation to explicitly control the fraction of active attention heads per token, with the target sparsity increasing on a cosine schedule. This allows the model to first learn rich attention patterns, then compress them into sparse, sink-free representations. Experiments: We train 1.7B dense models on 300B tokens (C4 + SlimPajama), comparing fixed sigmoid gating (anchor baseline), static sparse gating, and our dynamic scheduler. Evaluation covers perplexity on standard benchmarks, RULER long-context tasks (up to 128K tokens), attention sink diagnostics, and training stability metrics under varying learning rates. We ablate scheduler shape (linear, cosine, step) and target sparsity levels.

title: Adaptive Gate Temperature Scheduling: Dynamic Sparsity Control in Gated Attention for Continual Learning
description:
Problem: Large language models suffer from catastrophic forgetting during continual learning (sequential fine-tuning on new domains/tasks). Standard softmax attention uniformly attends across all heads, making it difficult to preserve previously learned representations. The gated attention framework—which introduces head-specific sigmoid gates creating sparse, query-dependent modulation—presents an underexplored opportunity: gates could selectively 'freeze' attention patterns for old knowledge while allowing new patterns to emerge.

Proposed Method: We introduce temperature-scheduled gated attention where each head maintains a learnable gate temperature parameter updated via meta-gradient signals reflecting task-specific forgetting metrics. During continual learning, heads with low gate entropy (specialized, sparse heads) receive reduced learning rates via a gate-anchoring loss, preserving their attention sink-free sparse patterns. New tasks preferentially recruit high-entropy (diffuse) heads. We add a gate orthogonality regularizer encouraging diverse specialization across heads.

Experiments: (1) Sequential fine-tuning on 5 diverse NLP benchmarks measuring forward transfer and backward interference; (2) Comparison against EWC, LoRA, and standard gated attention baselines on 1.7B dense models; (3) Ablation of temperature scheduling vs. fixed gates; (4) Visualization of per-head gate entropy evolution across tasks; (5) Long-context evaluation to verify attention-sink-free properties are preserved post-continual-training.

title: Adaptive Gate Pruning for Efficient Inference: Exploiting Sparse Gating Patterns in Gated Attention Transformers
description: Problem: While gated attention improves LLM quality by introducing query-dependent sparse gating scores, the computational overhead of computing these gates at inference time is non-trivial, and the induced sparsity is not yet exploited for actual hardware speedups. Existing attention sparsity methods (e.g., sparse transformers) rely on static or input-agnostic patterns, missing dynamic structure revealed by learned gates. Proposed Method: We investigate the empirical distribution of head-specific sigmoid gate activations across diverse inputs and model layers, identifying that a significant fraction of gates collapse near zero at inference time. We propose Gate-Guided Attention Pruning (GGAP): a two-stage approach where (1) a lightweight predictor—trained on gate activation statistics—forecasts which heads will produce near-zero gates before full SDPA computation, skipping those heads entirely, and (2) remaining active heads are computed with standard SDPA. The predictor uses only the query projection output, adding minimal latency. We further develop a calibration procedure to set per-layer sparsity thresholds balancing accuracy and speedup. Experiments: We evaluate on the released gated-attention MoE and dense models across standard benchmarks (MMLU, HellaSwag, GSM8K) and long-context tasks (RULER, LongBench), measuring accuracy-latency tradeoffs at 20–60% gate sparsity levels, comparing against static head pruning and H2O baselines on A100 hardware.

title: Adaptive Gating Topology Search for Heterogeneous Attention Heads: Learning When and Where to Gate
description:
Problem: The anchor paper identifies that a head-specific sigmoid gate post-SDPA consistently improves performance, but applies the same gating topology uniformly across all layers and heads. Different attention heads likely serve distinct functional roles (local vs. global attention, syntax vs. semantics), suggesting that heterogeneous gating strategies per head/layer could yield further gains.

Proposed Method: We propose a differentiable architecture search (DARTS-style) framework to jointly learn (1) gating position (pre-Q/K/V projection, post-SDPA, post-projection), (2) gating function type (sigmoid, tanh, SiLU, ReLU), and (3) gating granularity (head-specific, head-group, or layer-wide) for each attention head independently. During a warm-up phase on a proxy 400M model, a lightweight controller network trained with Gumbel-softmax relaxation selects the optimal gating topology per head.
