The discovered heterogeneous topology is then transferred to train 1.7B and 7B dense models from scratch.

Experiments: (1) Benchmark perplexity and downstream task accuracy vs. uniform gating baseline from anchor paper; (2) Analysis of discovered topology patterns across layers (early vs. late, shallow vs. deep); (3) Long-context extrapolation (128K tokens) measuring attention sink suppression; (4) Ablations on topology transfer across model scales; (5) Training stability and learning rate tolerance comparisons.

title: Adaptive Gate Pruning for Efficient Inference: Exploiting Sparsity Patterns in Gated Attention at Deployment Time
description: Problem: While the anchor paper demonstrates that head-specific sigmoid gating after SDPA improves training stability and mitigates attention sinks, the runtime sparsity induced by near-zero gate values represents an untapped computational efficiency opportunity. During inference, many gate activations collapse toward zero for specific heads and token positions, yet current implementations still compute full SDPA for those heads. Proposed Method: We propose Gate-Aware Dynamic Head Skipping (GADHS), a deployment-time optimization that predicts gate sparsity before executing SDPA. Specifically, we train lightweight per-head predictors (2-layer MLPs operating on query/key statistics) that estimate whether a gate will fall below a learned threshold τ_h, allowing early exit from full attention computation for that head. We further introduce a calibration procedure using a small representative dataset to set per-head thresholds balancing accuracy vs. skip rate. Unlike static pruning, GADHS adapts dynamically to input context. Planned Experiments: (1) Evaluate on pretrained gated-attention MoE and dense models released by the anchor paper; (2) Measure FLOPs reduction vs. perplexity degradation across thresholds on language modeling benchmarks (WikiText-103, C4); (3) Long-context benchmarks (SCROLLS, RULER) to verify that attention-sink-free properties are preserved under gating; (4) Latency profiling on A100/H100 GPUs demonstrating wall-clock speedups of 15-30% with <0.3 perplexity degradation.

title: Adaptive Gate Pruning for Efficient Inference: Exploiting Sparsity in Gated Attention at Deployment Time
description: Problem: While gated attention (GA) improves LLM training stability and long-context performance, its head-specific sigmoid gates introduce additional computation. However, the paper reveals that these gates produce sparse outputs—many heads receive near-zero gate values for given queries. This sparsity is currently unused during inference, leaving significant efficiency gains unrealized. Proposed Method: We propose GateSkip, a framework that exploits the dynamic sparsity of sigmoid gates to skip entire attention head computations at inference time. During a calibration phase on representative inputs, we profile per-head gate activation distributions and learn lightweight gate predictors (small linear probes on query projections) that predict whether a head's gate will fall below a threshold τ before computing full SDPA. Heads predicted as near-zero are skipped entirely, with their contribution replaced by a learned bias residual. We further propose a differentiable sparsity-aware fine-tuning objective to encourage gate distributions to be more bimodal, improving predictor accuracy without sacrificing model quality. Experiments: We evaluate GateSkip on the released 1.7B and 15B MoE gated attention models across standard benchmarks (MMLU, HellaSwag, LongBench), measuring FLOPs reduction, wall-clock speedup on A100/H100 GPUs, and quality degradation versus threshold τ. We compare against magnitude-based head pruning and static attention sparsity baselines, targeting >25% FLOPs reduction with <1% benchmark degradation.

title: Adaptive Gate Pruning: Learning When Gated Attention Heads Are Unnecessary
description:
Problem: While head-specific sigmoid gating after SDPA improves LLM performance, not all attention heads may benefit equally from gating. Some heads might learn near-constant gate values (always-on or always-off), contributing computational overhead without meaningful benefit. Understanding which heads genuinely leverage sparse, query-dependent gating versus those that behave like ungated attention could enable architectural compression and interpretability insights.

Proposed Method: We introduce Gated Attention with Learned Gate Sparsity (GALS), which augments the head-specific sigmoid gate with a differentiable binary concrete relaxation that allows gates to collapse to either a constant scalar or a query-dependent vector during training. We add a structured sparsity regularizer that penalizes gate variance across queries, encouraging heads to either fully commit to dynamic gating or fall back to static scaling. Post-training, heads with low gate variance are 'crystallized' into static scaling factors, reducing inference cost.

Experiments: (1) Train 1.7B dense models comparing baseline gated attention vs. GALS on standard language modeling benchmarks. (2) Analyze which layers/heads retain dynamic vs. static gates and correlate with attention patterns (sink heads, retrieval heads). (3) Evaluate inference throughput savings from gate crystallization. (4) Test long-context extrapolation to verify dynamic gates concentrate in sink-mitigation heads. Dataset: 500B tokens from FineWeb.

title: Adaptive Gate Temperature Scheduling: Dynamic Sparsity Control in Gated Attention for Efficient Long-Context Inference
description:
Problem: The sigmoid gate in gated attention applies uniform sparsity pressure across all layers, heads, and sequence positions. However, different heads specialize in local vs. global dependencies, and different layers process distinct abstraction levels—suggesting that static gating may leave performance on the table, particularly for long-context tasks where selective sparsity is critical for both efficiency and accuracy.

Proposed Method: We introduce layer-wise and head-wise learnable temperature parameters for the sigmoid gate, combined with a curriculum-based annealing schedule during training. Early training uses high temperature (near-linear gates) for stable optimization, gradually decreasing to promote sparse, specialized behavior. Additionally, we propose a position-aware gate modulation that scales gate activation based on relative token distance, enabling heads to adaptively trade off local versus global attention patterns without explicit architectural constraints.

Experiments: (1) Train 1.7B dense models with adaptive vs. fixed-temperature gated attention on 1T tokens, evaluating perplexity and downstream tasks. (2) Ablate temperature schedules (cosine, linear, step) and initialization strategies. (3) Evaluate long-context extrapolation on SCROLLS, RULER, and needle-in-haystack benchmarks up to 128K context. (4) Analyze emergent head specialization via gate activation statistics, measuring attention sink reduction quantitatively. (5) Measure inference FLOPs savings from induced sparsity versus performance trade-offs.

title: Adaptive Gate Calibration for Efficient Long-Context Retrieval: Learning When to Suppress Attention Sinks
description: Problem: While the anchor paper demonstrates that head-specific sigmoid gating after SDPA mitigates attention sinks and improves long-context extrapolation, the gating mechanism treats all sequence positions uniformly. In long-context retrieval tasks (e.g., needle-in-a-haystack, multi-hop reasoning over 128K+ tokens), selectively suppressing sink tokens while amplifying task-relevant positions could yield further gains, but the static sigmoid gate lacks dynamic positional awareness. Proposed Method: We introduce Position-Aware Adaptive Gating (PAAG), which augments the head-specific sigmoid gate with a lightweight positional scoring module trained to distinguish sink tokens from informative tokens. Specifically, PAAG learns a low-rank projection from query-key interaction patterns to produce a position-conditioned gate scalar, applied multiplicatively with the existing sigmoid gate. We additionally incorporate a sparsity regularization loss during fine-tuning to encourage the gate to zero out identified sink positions explicitly. This module adds negligible parameters (~0.01% overhead) and can be retrofitted onto pretrained gated-attention models. Experiments: (1) Fine-tune 1.7B dense models with PAAG on long-context SFT data; (2) Evaluate on RULER, LongBench, and needle-in-a-haystack benchmarks at 32K-256K context lengths; (3) Ablate gate sparsity regularization strength; (4) Visualize attention sink suppression via head-level attribution maps; (5) Compare inference throughput against sliding-window and StreamingLLM baselines.

title: Adaptive Gating Heads: Learning When to Gate in Heterogeneous Transformer Layers
description: Problem: The anchor paper applies a uniform head-specific sigmoid gate after SDPA across all layers and heads, but different layers serve distinct computational roles (early layers capture local syntax, later layers handle semantic composition). Applying identical gating schemes everywhere may be suboptimal—some heads may benefit from strong gating while others (e.g., induction heads or retrieval heads) may be harmed by sparsification. Proposed Method: We introduce Adaptive Gating Heads (AGH), where each attention head learns a continuous 'gating commitment' parameter during training that interpolates between no-gate, sigmoid-gate, and tanh-gate variants. A lightweight meta-network predicts per-layer gating intensity based on the layer's depth, hidden state statistics, and task signals. During training, gates are jointly optimized with model parameters via straight-through estimators for discrete commitment decisions. A regularization term encourages diverse gating strategies across layers. Experiments: (1) Train 1.7B dense models on 500B tokens comparing uniform gating vs. AGH; (2) Analyze which layer types adopt which gating behaviors via interpretability probes; (3) Evaluate long-context extrapolation (up to 128K tokens) and attention sink metrics; (4) Test transfer: fine-tune pretrained no-gate models by adding AGH adapters. We hypothesize AGH achieves better perplexity and long-context performance with fewer parameters dedicated to gating.

title: Adaptive Gating Frequency: Learning When Attention Needs Non-Linearity Across Layers and Heads
description:
Problem: The anchor paper establishes that head-specific sigmoid gating after SDPA consistently improves LLM performance by introducing non-linearity and sparse modulation. However, it applies gating uniformly across all layers and heads. Different layers encode syntactic vs. semantic vs. positional information at varying abstraction levels, suggesting that gating may be differentially beneficial—some layers/heads may already exhibit sufficient non-linearity while others critically need it. Applying uniform gating may waste parameters or even hurt specialized attention patterns.

Proposed Method: We introduce Heterogeneous Gated Attention (HGA), which learns a continuous gate-presence weight per layer and per head via differentiable binary concrete relaxation during training. This yields a sparse, learned gating topology rather than a fixed uniform one. We additionally analyze which layer/head types (induction heads, positional heads, semantic heads) preferentially retain gates post-training, connecting gating frequency to mechanistic interpretability.

Experiments: (1) Train 1.7B dense models with HGA vs. uniform gating vs. no gating on 500B tokens; (2) Evaluate perplexity, downstream benchmarks, attention-sink frequency, and long-context extrapolation (128K); (3) Ablate gate sparsity budgets (10%–100% of heads gated); (4) Probing classifiers to correlate retained gates with known head functional types; (5) Scaling analysis at 7B to validate topology generalization.

title: Adaptive Gate Calibration for Continual Learning: Leveraging Sparse Gating to Mitigate Catastrophic Forgetting in Large Language Models
description:
Problem: Catastrophic forgetting remains a critical challenge in continual learning (CL) for LLMs, where fine-tuning on new tasks degrades performance on previously learned ones. Existing methods (EWC, LoRA-based replay, parameter isolation) impose significant memory or computational overhead. The anchor paper demonstrates that head-specific sigmoid gates after SDPA produce sparse, query-dependent modulation patterns that mitigate attention sinks—suggesting these gates encode task-relevant structural information.

Proposed Method: We hypothesize that the sparse gating scores learned per attention head naturally encode task-specific attention routing. We propose GateCL: a continual learning framework that (1) freezes backbone weights after initial training, (2) learns lightweight task-specific gate vectors (one per head, ~0.01% parameters) for each new task, (3) uses gate activation divergence as a task-similarity signal for selective parameter sharing across tasks, and (4) employs a gate-guided elastic weight consolidation that protects parameters with high gate-activation variance across tasks.

Experiments: We evaluate on standard CL benchmarks (Split-CIFAR via language descriptions, SuperGLUE sequential tasks, domain-incremental instruction tuning). Metrics include backward/forward transfer, parameter efficiency, and perplexity on held-out long-context tasks. Ablations compare gate-only adaptation vs. LoRA, full fine-tuning, and prompt-tuning baselines across 5-20 sequential tasks.

title: Adaptive Gate Calibration for Continual Learning: Leveraging Sigmoid-Gated Attention to Mitigate Catastrophic Forgetting in LLMs
description:
Problem: Catastrophic forgetting remains a core challenge when continually fine-tuning LLMs on sequential task streams. Existing approaches (EWC, replay buffers, LoRA) impose external constraints without exploiting intrinsic architectural properties. The gated attention paper reveals that head-specific sigmoid gates produce sparse, query-dependent modulation that mitigates attention sinks and stabilizes training—properties potentially valuable for preserving prior task knowledge.

Proposed Method: We hypothesize that sigmoid gate activations encode task-specific attention patterns that are more compact and separable than full weight matrices. We propose GateCalib: (1) after learning each task, record per-head gate activation statistics (mean, variance) as lightweight task signatures; (2) during subsequent task training, penalize deviation from previous gate distributions using a KL-divergence regularizer applied exclusively to gate parameters, leaving value/query/key projections unconstrained; (3) optionally use gate signatures for zero-shot task identity inference to enable dynamic weight selection in a mixture-of-experts continual setting.

Experiments: (1) Sequential fine-tuning on 5-task NLP benchmarks (SuperGLUE tasks) comparing GateCalib vs. EWC, LoRA+replay, O-LoRA; (2) Ablations on gate regularization strength and scope; (3) Long-context task retention experiments; (4) Scaling analysis at 1.7B and 7B parameter regimes to validate gate separability across model sizes.

title: Adaptive Gate Pruning for Efficient Inference: Exploiting Sparsity in Gated Attention at Deployment Time
description:
Problem: While gated attention improves LLM quality by introducing query-dependent sparse gating scores over SDPA outputs, the computational overhead of gating remains constant at inference time, even when many gate values are near-zero. This represents an untapped opportunity: if gating naturally induces sparsity, we should exploit it to accelerate inference without quality loss.

Proposed Method: We introduce a dynamic gate-threshold inference framework that (1) profiles the empirical distribution of sigmoid gate activations across heads and layers during a calibration pass on representative data, (2) learns per-head sparsity thresholds that zero out low-magnitude gated attention contributions below a quality-preserving cutoff, and (3) implements a hardware-aware sparse accumulation kernel that skips masked head computations entirely. We further propose 'gate distillation': training a small predictor network that forecasts which heads will produce near-zero gates given only the query representation, enabling early exit before full SDPA computation.

Experiments: We evaluate on Llama-3-scale dense models (1.7B, 7B) pre-trained with post-hoc gating insertion versus natively trained gated models. Metrics include throughput (tokens/sec), memory bandwidth, perplexity degradation, and long-context benchmarks (RULER, SCROLLS). We analyze the gate-sparsity vs. accuracy Pareto frontier and compare against head pruning and attention approximation baselines.

title: Adaptive Gate Pruning: Exploiting Gated Attention Sparsity for Efficient Inference via Head-Level Dynamic Skipping
description: Problem: While gated softmax attention improves LLM quality and mitigates attention sinks, the computational cost of inference remains unchanged—the sigmoid gate scores are computed but the full SDPA is still executed regardless of gate magnitude. We hypothesize that the query-dependent sparse gating patterns identified in the anchor paper can be directly exploited to skip expensive attention computations at inference time. Method: We propose Adaptive Gate Pruning (AGP), which (1) trains a lightweight gate predictor (a small MLP per head using only the query vector) that predicts gate activation magnitudes before SDPA computation, (2) sets per-head dynamic thresholds calibrated on a small held-out set to achieve target sparsity levels, and (3) routes low-gate heads to a cheap linear approximation (single-vector attention) while routing high-gate heads to full SDPA. We also investigate whether gate sparsity correlates with token position, sequence length, and task type to enable structured skipping. Experiments: We evaluate on the released gated attention models (1.7B dense, 15B MoE) across LM benchmarks (MMLU, HellaSwag, GSM8K), long-context tasks (RULER, LongBench), and measure wall-clock inference speedup on A100s at various batch sizes and sequence lengths (1K–64K), targeting >20% FLOPs reduction with <1% quality degradation.

title: Adaptive Gate Calibration for Continual Learning: Leveraging Sparse Gating to Mitigate Catastrophic Forgetting in LLMs
description: Problem: Catastrophic forgetting remains a critical challenge when fine-tuning LLMs on sequential tasks. Current approaches (EWC, LoRA, replay buffers) either impose high computational overhead or require storing old data. The anchor paper shows that head-specific sigmoid gates after SDPA produce sparse, query-dependent modulation that suppresses attention sinks and improves generalization—suggesting these gate scores encode task-relevant attention patterns that could be exploited for continual learning. Proposed Method: We introduce Gate-Calibrated Continual Learning (GCCL), which (1) treats the learned sigmoid gate weights as lightweight task descriptors; (2) regularizes gate drift between sequential tasks using a Fisher-weighted gate-similarity penalty, preserving critical attention routing without full parameter regularization; (3) employs task-specific gate scaling vectors (low-rank, ~0.01% params) injected post-SDPA, enabling task switching via gate modulation rather than full adapter swapping. This leverages the sparsity property identified in the anchor paper—gates that are near-zero for one task can freely adapt for a new task with minimal interference. Experiments: We evaluate on standard continual learning benchmarks (Split-GLUE, Sequential SuperGLUE, domain-incremental code→math→reasoning), measuring forward transfer, backward transfer, and forgetting metrics. We compare against EWC, L2P, O-LoRA, and MoE-based continual learning baselines, ablating gate regularization strength and rank of task-specific scaling vectors across 1.7B and 7B model scales.

title: Adaptive Gating Schedules for Attention: Learning When to Be Sparse During Training
description: Problem: The anchor paper demonstrates that a fixed head-specific sigmoid gate after SDPA consistently improves LLM performance by introducing sparsity and eliminating attention sinks. However, applying full gating strength uniformly throughout training may be suboptimal—early training may benefit from denser attention to learn broad token associations, while later stages benefit from sparse, focused attention patterns. No work has examined whether dynamically scheduling gating intensity during training yields further improvements over static gating. Proposed Method: We introduce Curriculum Gating, where the sigmoid gate's temperature and/or a learned global scaling factor are annealed according to a schedule during training. Specifically, we parameterize the gate as σ(αt · hq), where αt follows a monotonically increasing curriculum (linear, cosine, or learned via a small meta-optimizer) from near-linear (dense) behavior early in training to strong sigmoid nonlinearity (sparse) later. We also explore per-layer and per-head curriculum rates discovered via differentiable scheduling. Experiments: We train 1.7B dense models on 500B tokens comparing (1) no gating, (2) static sigmoid gating (anchor paper baseline), (3) linear curriculum, (4) cosine curriculum, and (5) learned per-head curriculum. Evaluation covers perplexity, attention sink prevalence, long-context extrapolation (32K tokens), training stability under large LRs, and downstream benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, LongBench).

title: Adaptive Gate Calibration for Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Reducing Attention Sink in Long-Context Document Grounding
description:
Problem: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems struggle when relevant evidence is buried in long retrieved contexts, partly because attention sinks cause models to disproportionately attend to early tokens (e.g., BOS or query tokens) rather than dispersed evidence passages. The anchor paper shows sigmoid gating after SDPA mitigates attention sinks and improves long-context extrapolation, but this has not been studied in the RAG setting where context structure (query + multiple retrieved chunks) creates distinct distributional patterns.

Proposed Method: We introduce Retrieval-Aware Gated Attention (RAGA), which augments the head-specific sigmoid gate with a lightweight chunk-boundary signal. Specifically, we inject learned positional embeddings at chunk boundaries and condition the gate scalar on both the head representation and a chunk-ID embedding, allowing the model to adaptively suppress sink formation at document boundaries. During fine-tuning on RAG tasks, gates are trained to promote within-chunk local attention concentration on relevant spans while suppressing cross-chunk sink accumulation.

Experiments: (1) Fine-tune a 7B baseline with and without RAGA on MSMARCO and Natural Questions in a multi-document RAG setup; (2) Evaluate on SCROLLS, RULER, and a new 128K-token needle-in-haystack RAG benchmark; (3) Analyze attention sink frequency per chunk position with and without RAGA; (4) Ablate chunk-boundary conditioning vs. vanilla sigmoid gate from the anchor paper.

title: Adaptive Gating Schedules for Attention: Learning When Sparsity Matters Across Layers and Training Stages
description: Problem: The anchor paper applies uniform sigmoid gating across all attention heads post-SDPA, but attention sink patterns and sparsity requirements vary substantially across layers (early layers capture local syntax; late layers handle long-range semantics) and across training stages (early training needs dense gradient flow; later stages benefit from sparsity). A static, uniform gating strategy may be suboptimal across this heterogeneity. Proposed Method: We introduce Layer-Adaptive Gated Attention (LAGA), which learns per-layer gating hyperparameters (sparsity temperature, gate initialization bias) through a meta-learning outer loop that optimizes validation perplexity. During training, we anneal gate temperatures layer-specifically using a curriculum: initially biasing gates toward dense attention (near-linear activations) and progressively encouraging sparsity. We also introduce a layer-depth-conditioned gating module that shares parameters across layers via a lightweight MLP taking normalized layer index as input. Experiments: We train 1.7B dense models on 500B tokens, comparing (1) uniform sigmoid gating (anchor baseline), (2) manually designed layer-wise schedules, and (3) LAGA. We evaluate perplexity, attention sink frequency per layer, long-context extrapolation (4k→32k), and training stability under large learning rates. Ablations examine temperature curriculum design and parameter sharing strategies across layers.

title: Adaptive Gate Sparsity via Learned Thresholds: Connecting Gated Attention to Dynamic Token Pruning
description: Problem: The gated attention mechanism improves LLM performance by introducing query-dependent sparsity, but the sparsity pattern emerges implicitly from sigmoid activations without explicit control. This makes it difficult to trade off computation against quality at inference time, and leaves unclear how gate sparsity relates to established token/head pruning methods. Proposed Method: We augment the head-specific sigmoid gate with a lightweight learned threshold module that explicitly controls gate sparsity per head per layer. Specifically, after computing sigmoid gate scores, we apply a differentiable straight-through top-k or learned scalar threshold that zeroes out low-scoring heads during both training and inference. We train sparsity-rate embeddings conditioned on sequence position and layer depth, enabling dynamic computation budgets. We also analyze the correlation between gate sparsity patterns and traditional attention-sink positions to validate that explicit sparsity control further suppresses sink formation. Experiments: (1) Train 1.7B dense models at 200B tokens comparing implicit sigmoid gating vs. our explicit adaptive-threshold gating across 3–5 target sparsity levels (10%–50%). (2) Evaluate perplexity, long-context extrapolation (up to 128K tokens), and attention-sink prevalence. (3) Measure wall-clock inference speedup using sparse CUDA kernels. (4) Ablate threshold conditioning signals (layer, position, content-dependent).

title: Adaptive Gate Calibration for Cross-Layer Attention Sharing in Efficient LLMs
description: Problem: Large language models increasingly adopt cross-layer attention (CLA) or grouped-layer attention to reduce KV-cache memory, but sharing attention states across layers degrades model quality because different layers capture distinct linguistic abstractions. Standard gating (as studied in the anchor paper) is applied uniformly per head within a single layer, leaving cross-layer interference unaddressed. Proposed Method: We introduce Layer-Adaptive Gated Attention (LAGA), where each layer that receives a shared KV-cache from an earlier donor layer applies a learned sigmoid gate conditioned on both the current query and a lightweight layer-identity embedding. This gate dynamically suppresses or amplifies shared attention outputs based on layer depth and input context, effectively letting each consumer layer 'unshare' irrelevant donor attention patterns on-the-fly. We further analyze whether LAGA's sparsity reduces attention sinks propagated through shared KV caches, hypothesizing that sink tokens in donor layers corrupt consumer layers disproportionately. Experiments: We train 1B and 3B parameter models with 2:1 CLA ratios on 500B tokens (FineWeb), comparing baselines (CLA without gating, uniform sigmoid gate, no sharing) against LAGA on standard benchmarks (MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC), long-context tasks (RULER), and KV-cache memory profiling. Ablations vary gate conditioning signals and sharing ratios.

title: Adaptive Gating Schedules for Attention: Learning When to Be Sparse During Training
description: Problem: The anchor paper demonstrates that a fixed head-specific sigmoid gate after SDPA consistently improves performance, but treats gating as a static architectural choice. We hypothesize that the optimal gating behavior evolves during training—early stages may benefit from denser attention for gradient flow and feature discovery, while later stages benefit from sparsity for generalization and attention-sink mitigation. Proposed Method: We introduce Curriculum Gating, a dynamic training strategy where the sigmoid gate's temperature and initialization are scheduled across training. Specifically, we parameterize the gate as σ(α·g_h), where α is a learnable or schedule-driven temperature parameter that begins near zero (near-uniform gating) and gradually increases (sharper, sparser gating) following a cosine or step-wise curriculum. We also explore per-layer and per-head differentiated schedules derived from gradient signal magnitudes. Planned Experiments: (1) Train 1.7B dense models on 100B tokens comparing fixed gates, random schedules, and curriculum schedules across perplexity and downstream benchmarks; (2) Analyze attention sink emergence/disappearance during training under different schedules; (3) Evaluate long-context extrapolation (4k→32k) for models trained with curriculum vs. fixed gating; (4) Ablate temperature schedule shapes and initialization strategies to identify robust recipes.

title: Adaptive Gating for Multimodal Attention: Suppressing Cross-Modal Attention Sinks in Vision-Language Models
description: Problem: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) suffer from cross-modal attention sinks, where attention heads disproportionately focus on a small number of image tokens (often patch boundary tokens) or special delimiter tokens, degrading fine-grained visual grounding and long-context visual reasoning. Standard softmax attention in VLMs inherits this pathology but gating mechanisms tailored for multimodal cross-attention remain unexplored. Proposed Method: We extend head-specific sigmoid gating to multimodal attention layers, introducing modality-aware gating that applies distinct learned gates for self-attention within each modality versus cross-modal attention between vision and language tokens. Specifically, we add a lightweight query-dependent gate computed from the language query stream to modulate the cross-attention output over visual tokens, enabling sparsity that suppresses uninformative visual sinks. We additionally propose a 'modality gate' that learns to dynamically balance how much visual versus linguistic context each head attends to. Experiments: We train 1.7B and 7B VLMs on image-text interleaved data, comparing baseline softmax, uniform sigmoid gating, and our modality-aware gating. Evaluations target: (1) visual grounding benchmarks (RefCOCO, VQAv2), (2) long-context visual document understanding (DocVQA, MMLongBench-Doc), (3) attention sink analysis via attention entropy metrics, and (4) scaling behavior up to 72B parameters using MoE.

title: Adaptive Gating Geometry: Learning Head-Wise Gate Structures for Heterogeneous Attention Specialization
description:
Problem: The anchor paper shows that a head-specific sigmoid gate after SDPA consistently improves LLM performance, but treats all attention heads homogeneously — each head receives the same gate architecture. Yet, empirical evidence suggests different heads specialize in distinct functions (syntactic, semantic, positional, retrieval), implying that optimal gating geometry may vary across heads and layers.

Proposed Method: We introduce Adaptive Gating Geometry (AGG), which learns per-head gate structures from a differentiable family of gating functions parameterized by (1) gate activation type (sigmoid, tanh, ReLU, SiLU), (2) gate input source (query, key, value, or their combinations), and (3) gate rank (scalar, vector, low-rank matrix). Using a lightweight Neural Architecture Search (NAS) with Gumbel-softmax relaxation during a short warm-up phase, we discover heterogeneous gate configurations per head. The final architecture is then trained from scratch using the discovered per-head gates.

Experiments: We train 1.7B dense models on 500B tokens, comparing: (1) uniform sigmoid gate baseline from anchor paper, (2) AGG-discovered heterogeneous gates, (3) ablations fixing each dimension independently. Evaluation covers standard LM benchmarks, long-context extrapolation (up to 128K tokens), attention sink analysis, and head specialization probing. We hypothesize heterogeneous gating improves long-context tasks by 3-5% over the uniform baseline while reducing attention sink phenomena further.

title: Adaptive Gating Schedules for Attention: Dynamic Sparsity Control During Training and Inference
description:
Problem: The anchor paper demonstrates that a fixed head-specific sigmoid gate after SDPA consistently improves LLM performance by inducing sparsity and eliminating attention sinks. However, the optimal degree of sparsity likely varies across training stages (early dense exploration vs. late specialization), sequence positions, and task types. A static gating mechanism cannot adapt to these varying requirements, potentially leaving performance on the table.

Proposed Method: We introduce Adaptive Gating Schedules (AGS), which parameterize the sigmoid gate's temperature and bias as learnable functions of (1) training step via a scheduled annealing curriculum, (2) layer depth through layer-conditioned hypernetworks, and (3) input context statistics via a lightweight router. During inference, we add a task-adaptive gating mode that adjusts sparsity based on detected task type (retrieval vs. generation vs. reasoning). The gate parameters are meta-learned using a small held-out validation loss signal, analogous to curriculum learning.

Experiments: (1) Train 1.7B dense models comparing static gates vs. AGS variants on the same 3.5T token corpus. (2) Ablate scheduling components (training-stage vs. layer-depth vs. context-adaptive). (3) Evaluate long-context extrapolation (128K tokens), attention sink metrics, and few-shot benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, RULER). (4) Analyze learned sparsity patterns across layers and training stages to characterize emergent specialization.

title: Adaptive Gate Calibration for Cross-Lingual Transfer: Probing Whether Gated Attention Reduces Representational Anisotropy Across Languages
description: Problem: Large multilingual LLMs suffer from representational anisotropy and uneven cross-lingual alignment, partly attributed to attention sinks concentrating on language-specific tokens. The anchor paper shows that head-specific sigmoid gating after SDPA mitigates attention sinks and improves long-context extrapolation—yet its impact on multilingual representation quality and cross-lingual transfer remains unexplored. Proposed Method: We train matched pairs of standard softmax-attention and gated-attention (post-SDPA sigmoid) multilingual models at 1.7B scale on a balanced 500B token multilingual corpus (covering 30 languages). We introduce a language-conditioned gate calibration technique where gate biases are initialized per language family using small adapter parameters, allowing the sparsity induced by gating to align across typologically diverse languages without full retraining. We analyze (1) isotropy of hidden representations per language via singular value entropy, (2) attention sink distribution across languages, and (3) zero-shot cross-lingual transfer on XNLI, MLQA, and XStoryCloze. Experiments: Ablations compare vanilla softmax, post-SDPA sigmoid gate (anchor finding), and our language-conditioned calibrated gate. We measure scaling behavior (300M–1.7B), transfer gap between high/low-resource languages, and few-shot prompting robustness. We hypothesize gating reduces anisotropy uniformly and that calibration further closes the cross-lingual gap by 15–25%.

title: Adaptive Gate Calibration for Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Leveraging Sparse Gating to Suppress Context Noise
description:
Problem: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems suffer from attention sinks and irrelevant context pollution, where LLMs over-attend to positional artifacts or noisy retrieved passages rather than genuinely relevant tokens. The gated attention work demonstrates that head-specific sigmoid gates reduce attention sinks and improve long-context extrapolation—properties directly useful for RAG but unexplored in that setting.

Proposed Method: We introduce Retrieval-Aware Gated Attention (RAGA), which augments the sigmoid gate from the anchor paper with a lightweight relevance signal derived from the query-document similarity scores already computed during retrieval. Specifically, the gate bias is conditioned on per-passage retrieval scores injected as soft modifiers into the sigmoid gate activations, encouraging the model to sparsely attend within high-relevance passages and suppress low-relevance ones. No additional parameters beyond a small MLP projector are required.

Experiments: (1) Fine-tune 1.7B dense models (with and without gated attention) on KILT and BEIR benchmarks with varying retrieval quality (top-1 to top-10 passages, including noisy retrievals). (2) Ablate gate conditioning strategies: no conditioning, score-shift, score-scale, and combined. (3) Evaluate attention sink frequency in RAG contexts versus baseline. (4) Test long-context RAG on SCROLLS and RULER with 32K context windows. Metrics: exact match, F1, and attention entropy.

title: Adaptive Gate Pruning for Efficient Inference: Exploiting Sparsity in Gated Softmax Attention
description:
Problem: While gated softmax attention improves LLM quality and mitigates attention sinks, the added sigmoid gating operation introduces overhead during inference. However, the paper's finding that gating produces query-dependent sparse scores suggests a compelling opportunity: heads with near-zero gate outputs can be skipped entirely during decoding, enabling dynamic computation reduction without sacrificing model quality.

Proposed Method: We propose Gate-Driven Attention Sparsity (GDAS), a post-training inference optimization framework for gated attention models. During a calibration pass, we profile per-head gate activation distributions to identify 'consistently sparse' heads and establish per-head thresholding policies. At inference time, heads whose predicted gate magnitude falls below a learned threshold are skipped, with outputs replaced by cached or zero tensors. We additionally propose a lightweight gate predictor—a small MLP trained on query statistics—that forecasts gate sparsity before computing full SDPA, enabling early exit for sparse heads.

Experiments: (1) Evaluate throughput/latency speedup on gated MoE and dense models from the anchor paper across sequence lengths 1K-128K; (2) Measure perplexity degradation and downstream task accuracy under varying sparsity budgets; (3) Compare against static head pruning and H2O attention baselines; (4) Ablate gate predictor accuracy vs. oracle sparsity; (5) Analyze interaction between gate sparsity and long-context extrapolation quality.

title: Adaptive Gate Temperature Scheduling for Gated Attention: Dynamic Sparsity Control During Training
description:
Problem: The sigmoid gate in gated attention introduces fixed-temperature sparsity throughout training. However, optimal sparsity levels likely differ across training phases—early training may benefit from denser attention to build broad representations, while later stages benefit from sparser, more specialized patterns. No principled method exists for dynamically controlling gate sparsity during training.

Proposed Method: We introduce temperature-modulated gated attention, where the sigmoid gate operates as sigmoid(x/τ(t)), with τ(t) following a learned or scheduled annealing curriculum. We explore three variants: (1) fixed cosine annealing from high-to-low temperature (dense-to-sparse), (2) layer-wise adaptive temperatures updated via meta-gradient signals monitoring attention entropy, and (3) task-aware temperature conditioned on perplexity trajectory. We additionally investigate per-head temperature parameters that are trained end-to-end, allowing the model to self-organize sparse vs. dense heads.

Experiments: We train 1.7B dense models on 300B tokens, comparing against the fixed-sigmoid baseline from the anchor paper. Evaluations cover: (1) standard language modeling benchmarks, (2) long-context extrapolation (8K→32K), (3) attention sink prevalence metrics, (4) training stability under large learning rates, and (5) analysis of emergent head specialization patterns. We hypothesize dynamic sparsity scheduling improves both convergence speed and final benchmark performance while further reducing attention sink artifacts.

title: Adaptive Gating Geometry: Learning Head-Specific Gate Architectures via Neural Architecture Search for Heterogeneous Attention
description:
Problem: The anchor paper demonstrates that a uniform head-specific sigmoid gate after SDPA consistently improves LLM performance, but applies the same gating geometry to all attention heads. However, different heads serve distinct roles (local vs. global attention, syntactic vs. semantic), suggesting heterogeneous gating architectures could further improve performance and efficiency.

Proposed Method: We introduce Heterogeneous Gated Attention (HGA), which employs a differentiable NAS framework to jointly learn per-head gate architectures alongside model weights. Each head selects from a candidate gate space: (1) no gate, (2) sigmoid gate (as in anchor), (3) tanh gate, (4) low-rank factored gate with bottleneck, and (5) multi-layer MLP gate. We use a Gumbel-softmax relaxation to make architecture selection differentiable, enabling end-to-end training. After convergence, we discretize the architecture and fine-tune.

Experiments: (1) Train 1.3B dense models on 300B tokens, comparing HGA against uniform gating baselines across all gate types. (2) Analyze emergent head-type distributions and their correlation with known attention head roles. (3) Evaluate long-context extrapolation (up to 128K tokens) and attention sink mitigation. (4) Measure training stability across varying learning rates. (5) Ablate NAS overhead vs. performance gain trade-offs.

title: Adaptive Gate Calibration for Efficient Long-Context Retrieval: Learning When to Suppress Attention Sinks Dynamically
description: Problem: While gated attention with sigmoid post-SDPA gates mitigates attention sinks and improves long-context extrapolation, the gating mechanism is applied uniformly regardless of context length or token retrieval difficulty. In retrieval-intensive tasks (e.g., needle-in-a-haystack, multi-hop QA), fixed gate parameters may over-suppress relevant tokens or under-suppress sink tokens depending on position and query complexity. Method: We propose Context-Adaptive Gated Attention (CAGA), which augments the head-specific sigmoid gate with a lightweight meta-gating network that conditions gate scaling on (1) relative positional distance between query and key, (2) local attention entropy as a proxy for sink presence, and (3) a learned difficulty signal derived from the query representation norm. The meta-network adds <0.1% parameters and is trained with a sparsity-encouraging auxiliary loss that explicitly penalizes attention sink concentration. Experiments: We train 1.7B dense models on 3.5T tokens (matching anchor baselines), evaluating on: standard LM perplexity, RULER long-context benchmarks (8K-128K), passkey retrieval, multi-hop reasoning (HotpotQA, MuSiQue), and attention sink visualization. We ablate each conditioning signal, compare against fixed sigmoid gates and ALiBi/RoPE baselines, and analyze gate sparsity patterns across layers and heads at varying context lengths.

title: Adaptive Gate Calibration for Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Suppressing Context Dilution via Learned Sparsity
description:
Problem: In Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), LLMs often suffer from 'context dilution' where retrieved passages compete with parametric knowledge, leading to either ignoring relevant context or over-relying on noisy retrievals. The anchor paper shows that head-specific sigmoid gates reduce attention sinks and enable query-dependent sparse modulation—suggesting gating could selectively amplify attended context vs. parametric pathways.

Proposed Method: We introduce RAG-Gate, a lightweight modification that augments gated softmax attention with a retrieval-awareness signal. Specifically, we add a secondary gate conditioned on whether tokens belong to retrieved context segments (via positional segment embeddings), allowing the model to learn head-specific policies for when to trust retrieval vs. internal knowledge. The gate outputs are regularized with a sparsity loss that encourages specialization: some heads become 'retrieval heads' and others become 'memory heads.' Unlike prior retrieval-specific architectures, RAG-Gate requires no architectural overhaul—only the gate conditioning is modified.

Experiments: (1) Fine-tune 7B base models with RAG-Gate on KILT benchmark tasks; (2) Measure context utilization via counterfactual retrieval experiments; (3) Analyze head specialization emergence through gate activation statistics; (4) Test out-of-distribution retrieval quality degradation robustness; (5) Compare against CAT, RETRO, and standard RAG baselines on NaturalQuestions, TriviaQA, and PopQA.

title: Adaptive Gate Annealing: Dynamic Sparsity Scheduling in Gated Attention for Continual Pre-training and Domain Adaptation
description: Problem: While gated softmax attention improves base pre-training, it remains unclear how the learned gate sparsity evolves during continual pre-training or domain adaptation (e.g., shifting from general web text to code, math, or biomedical corpora). Static gating may over-suppress domain-specific attention patterns or fail to redistribute attention sinks appropriately when the data distribution shifts abruptly. Proposed Method: We introduce Gate Annealing Schedules (GAS), a framework that dynamically regulates the entropy/sparsity of sigmoid head gates during training phases. Concretely, we add a lightweight regularization term on gate activation distributions whose strength is annealed according to a curriculum tied to domain mixing ratios. We additionally propose Gate Transfer Initialization (GTI), which re-initializes gate parameters using statistics from source-domain checkpoints to preserve previously learned sparse patterns while allowing targeted redistribution. Planned Experiments: (1) Continual pre-training of a 1.7B gated-attention model from general text toward code/math domains, comparing GAS against frozen gates, fine-tuned gates, and standard softmax attention baselines. (2) Ablations on annealing schedule shape and regularization coefficient. (3) Analysis of attention sink evolution across domain transitions via gate activation histograms. (4) Long-context benchmarks (RULER, SCROLLS) to verify that domain-adapted models retain extrapolation benefits.

title: Adaptive Gate Temperature: Learning Per-Head Sparsity Schedules for Gated Attention Across Context Lengths
description:
Problem: The sigmoid gate introduced after SDPA improves sparsity and eliminates attention sinks, but uses a fixed implicit temperature. Different attention heads serve distinct functions (local syntactic, global semantic, positional) that likely benefit from different sparsity levels—and optimal sparsity may shift as context length grows. A static gate cannot adapt to these varying demands, potentially leaving performance on the table especially in long-context settings.

Proposed Method: We introduce Adaptive Temperature Gated Attention (ATGA), which augments each head's sigmoid gate with a learnable per-head temperature parameter that is further modulated by a lightweight MLP conditioned on current sequence length and head utilization statistics (computed via EMA during training). This allows each head to dynamically interpolate between near-binary sparse gating and softer gating regimes. We additionally propose a temperature regularization loss encouraging diversity across heads within each layer to prevent collapse.

Experiments: (1) Train 1.7B dense models on 500B tokens, comparing baseline softmax, fixed sigmoid gate, and ATGA on standard language modeling benchmarks. (2) Evaluate long-context extrapolation on SCROLLS, RULER, and passkey retrieval at 4K–128K tokens. (3) Analyze learned temperature distributions per head and layer to understand emergent specialization. (4) Ablate MLP conditioning vs. static per-head temperatures to isolate contributions.

title: Adaptive Gating Schedules for Attention: Dynamic Sparsity Control During Training and Inference
description:
Problem: The anchor paper demonstrates that a fixed sigmoid gate after SDPA consistently improves LLM performance by introducing sparsity and mitigating attention sinks. However, the optimal degree of gating sparsity likely varies across training stages, input contexts, and layer depths—a static gate cannot adapt to these dynamics. Early training may benefit from denser attention for gradient flow, while later stages and longer contexts profit from sparser patterns.

Proposed Method: We introduce Adaptive Gated Attention (AGA), which replaces the fixed sigmoid gate with a learnable schedule that controls gate temperature as a function of (1) training step, (2) layer index, and (3) sequence position. Specifically, we parameterize gate sparsity via a temperature-scaled sigmoid whose temperature is modulated by a small auxiliary network taking normalized training progress, layer depth, and local context entropy as inputs. During inference, we additionally propose a context-length-aware gate scaling that progressively sharpens gates as sequence length increases, explicitly targeting long-context extrapolation.

Experiments: We train 1.7B dense models on 500B tokens comparing static gated attention vs. AGA variants across multiple temperature schedules. Evaluations cover standard benchmarks (MMLU, HellaSwag), long-context tasks (SCROLLS, RULER at 32K/128K), attention sink visualization, training loss curves, and learning rate sensitivity. We ablate each conditioning signal (step, layer, entropy) independently to quantify contributions.

title: Adaptive Gating Frequency Across Layers: Learning When Softmax Attention Needs Non-linearity
description: Problem: The anchor paper applies head-specific sigmoid gating uniformly after SDPA across all layers and heads. However, different layers in transformers are known to serve distinct functional roles (e.g., early layers capture syntactic patterns, middle layers semantic reasoning, later layers task-specific representations). Applying gating uniformly may be suboptimal — some layers may benefit strongly from the non-linearity and sparsity introduced by gating, while others may not. Proposed Method: We introduce a learnable layer-wise and head-wise gating temperature/amplitude controller that determines how 'active' the sigmoid gate is per layer. Specifically, we parameterize each gate with a learned scalar α per layer that interpolates between a fully active gate (α=1) and a bypass (α=0), trained end-to-end. We further analyze the emergent gating patterns using gradient-based importance scores to understand which layers naturally suppress gating. Additionally, we explore whether attention sinks concentrate in specific layers and whether those layers exhibit weaker learned gating. Experiments: We train 1.7B dense models on 500B tokens, comparing uniform gating (baseline from anchor), our adaptive scheme, and no-gating baselines across standard benchmarks (MMLU, HellaSwag, GSM8K), long-context tasks (SCROLLS, RULER), and training stability metrics under varying learning rates.

title: Adaptive Gate Calibration for Continual Learning: Leveraging Sparse Gating to Mitigate Catastrophic Forgetting in LLMs
description: Problem: Continual learning in LLMs suffers from catastrophic forgetting, where fine-tuning on new tasks degrades performance on previously learned ones. Existing methods (EWC, replay, LoRA-based) add overhead or require storing old data. The anchor paper shows that head-specific sigmoid gates after SDPA induce query-dependent sparsity and mitigate attention sinks—properties that could be exploited to selectively protect task-critical attention patterns during sequential fine-tuning. Proposed Method: We introduce Gate-Calibrated Continual Learning (GCCL), which (1) identifies task-specific attention head importance via gate activation statistics on a held-out task buffer, (2) freezes or regularizes gates corresponding to high-importance heads for prior tasks while allowing full plasticity on low-importance heads for new tasks, and (3) uses a lightweight gate-distillation loss that preserves the sparse gating distributions of old tasks without storing raw data. The approach requires no architectural changes beyond the sigmoid gates already proposed in the anchor work. Experiments: We evaluate on standard continual learning benchmarks (Split-GLUE, SuperNLI sequences, domain-incremental language modeling) using pretrained gated-attention models at 1.7B scale. Metrics include backward transfer, forward transfer, and average accuracy. We compare against EWC, L2-regularization, LoRA-based continual methods, and vanilla fine-tuning baselines.

title: Adaptive Gate Annealing: Dynamic Sparsity Schedules for Gated Attention During Pretraining
description:
Problem: The anchor paper demonstrates that a fixed sigmoid gate after SDPA consistently improves LLM performance by inducing sparsity and mitigating attention sinks. However, it treats the gating mechanism as static throughout training, ignoring the possibility that optimal gate behavior may differ across training phases—early training benefits from dense attention for representation learning, while later stages benefit from sparse, focused attention for generalization.

Proposed Method: We propose Adaptive Gate Annealing (AGA), where the sigmoid gate's temperature and bias are dynamically scheduled during pretraining. Specifically, we introduce a learnable per-head temperature parameter τ that is jointly trained with a curriculum: starting high (near-uniform gates) and annealing toward lower values (sparse gates) following a cosine schedule. We also investigate data-adaptive gating where gate sparsity targets are conditioned on domain-specific token statistics detected via lightweight classifiers.

Experiments: (1) Train 1.7B dense models with static vs. annealed gates on 300B tokens, evaluating perplexity, downstream benchmarks, and attention sink metrics. (2) Ablate annealing schedules (linear, cosine, step) and starting temperatures. (3) Evaluate long-context extrapolation (up to 128K tokens) using RULER benchmark. (4) Analyze emergent sparsity patterns across layers and heads to characterize when/where dynamic gating matters most. Baseline comparisons include the anchor paper's best static variant and standard softmax attention.

title: Adaptive Gate Calibration for Efficient Long-Context Retrieval: Learning When to Suppress Attention Sinks Dynamically
description:
Problem: While head-specific sigmoid gating mitigates attention sinks and improves long-context extrapolation, the gate is applied uniformly regardless of whether a token is acting as a sink or carrying genuine semantic content. This uniform suppression may inadvertently dampen useful aggregation patterns in short-range tasks while being insufficient for very long sequences (>100K tokens) where sink formation dynamics differ across layers and heads.

Proposed Method: We introduce Content-Aware Adaptive Gating (CAAG), which replaces the fixed head-specific sigmoid gate with a lightweight meta-predictor that estimates per-token sink probability from key-query statistics (e.g., key norm, attention entropy) and modulates gate strength accordingly. The meta-predictor is a 2-layer MLP trained jointly with the LLM using a dual objective: standard language modeling loss plus an auxiliary contrastive loss that pushes sink tokens toward low gate values and semantic pivot tokens toward higher gate values, using synthetic sink labels derived from attention pattern analysis.

Experiments: (1) Train 1.7B dense models on 200B tokens, comparing baseline softmax, uniform sigmoid gate, and CAAG on standard benchmarks (MMLU, HellaSwag). (2) Evaluate long-context retrieval on SCROLLS and Needle-in-a-Haystack at 32K, 64K, 128K context lengths. (3) Ablate meta-predictor input features and auxiliary loss weight. (4) Analyze gate value distributions across layers to verify selective sink suppression.

title: Adaptive Gate Pruning for Efficient Long-Context Inference: Exploiting Sparsity in Gated Attention
description:
Problem: While gated softmax attention improves quality and mitigates attention sinks, the sigmoid gate introduces per-head sparse activation patterns that remain unexploited during inference. Existing KV-cache compression methods (H2O, StreamingLLM) rely on attention score heuristics, but the head-specific gate values in gated attention provide a cleaner, query-dependent sparsity signal that could enable more principled token eviction and KV-cache reduction.

Proposed Method: We propose Gate-Guided KV Eviction (GGKE), which uses the sigmoid gate activations as first-class citizens for dynamic KV-cache pruning. Specifically, tokens whose cumulative gate contribution across recent queries falls below an adaptive threshold are evicted from the KV cache. We further propose a gate-calibrated attention sink detector that identifies sink tokens via persistent high gate variance rather than high attention scores, enabling their retention or redistribution. Finally, we introduce a lightweight gate predictor module trained to forecast gate sparsity patterns one step ahead, enabling speculative cache pre-eviction.

Experiments: (1) Perplexity and accuracy on LongBench, RULER, and Needle-in-a-Haystack with varying cache budgets. (2) Comparison against H2O, SnapKV, and StreamingLLM baselines. (3) Inference throughput benchmarks at 32K–128K context lengths. (4) Ablations on gate threshold scheduling and the gate predictor accuracy-efficiency tradeoff. Models: 1.7B and 7B gated-attention LLMs from the anchor paper's released checkpoints.

title: Adaptive Gating Topology Search for Heterogeneous Attention Heads: Finding Optimal Per-Layer Gate Placement via Differentiable Architecture Search
description: Problem: The anchor paper demonstrates that a head-specific sigmoid gate after SDPA consistently improves LLM performance, but applies the same gating topology uniformly across all layers. Different layers in transformers are known to serve distinct functional roles (local vs. global attention, syntactic vs. semantic), suggesting that optimal gate placement and type may vary per layer or even per head. Treating all layers identically may leave performance gains unrealized. Proposed Method: We formulate gating topology selection as a differentiable neural architecture search (DNAS) problem. Each attention layer maintains a learned mixture over candidate gating variants (post-SDPA sigmoid, pre-SDPA query gate, value gate, no gate) parameterized by Gumbel-softmax relaxations. After a warm-up phase, architecture parameters are jointly optimized with model weights. We then discretize the architecture and perform a short fine-tuning stage. This yields a heterogeneous gating topology where each layer independently selects its optimal gate configuration. Experiments: We train 1.7B dense models on 500B tokens (matching anchor scale), comparing (1) uniform best-gate baseline from anchor, (2) our DNAS-discovered heterogeneous topology, and (3) random heterogeneous assignment. We analyze which layers select which gates, correlating choices with probing-based functional layer analysis, and evaluate on standard benchmarks plus long-context extrapolation tasks to measure attention-sink mitigation across topology types.

title: Dynamic Gate Calibration for Cross-Layer Attention Sharing in Long-Context LLMs
description:
Problem: Large language models struggle with efficient long-context processing because each layer independently computes full attention, leading to quadratic memory scaling. While gated attention improves per-layer quality (as shown in the anchor paper), it remains unclear how sigmoid gates interact across layers and whether gate patterns can be exploited for cross-layer KV-cache compression.

Proposed Method: We introduce Cross-Layer Gated Attention (CLGA), which leverages the observation that head-specific sigmoid gates naturally produce sparse, query-dependent activation patterns. We propose learning a gate-similarity metric between layers to identify which attention heads across adjacent layers produce structurally similar gating distributions. When two heads exhibit high gate correlation, we share their KV caches, using the gate values themselves as dynamic routing signals to modulate the shared cache contribution. A lightweight calibration network adjusts for distributional drift between layers. This transforms gate sparsity from a per-layer benefit into a cross-layer compression mechanism.

Experiments: (1) Train 1.7B and 7B models with CLGA on 2T tokens, comparing perplexity against baseline gated attention and standard attention. (2) Evaluate on long-context benchmarks (RULER, LongBench) at 32K-128K context lengths. (3) Measure KV-cache memory reduction and throughput gains. (4) Ablate gate-similarity thresholds and calibration network architectures. (5) Analyze attention-sink mitigation properties inherited from the anchor paper's findings.

title: Adaptive Gate Temperature Scheduling: Dynamic Sparsity Control in Gated Attention for Curriculum Learning
description:
Problem: The anchor paper shows sigmoid-gated attention improves performance by inducing sparsity and eliminating attention sinks, but uses a fixed gating mechanism throughout training. We hypothesize that the optimal sparsity level in gated attention should evolve during training—early stages benefit from denser attention for broad pattern acquisition, while later stages benefit from sparser, more specialized attention patterns.

Proposed Method: We introduce a learnable temperature parameter τ(t) that modulates the sigmoid gate: gate = σ(x/τ(t)), where τ follows a scheduled annealing from high values (near-uniform gates, dense attention) to low values (near-binary gates, sparse attention). We explore three scheduling strategies: (1) monotonic cosine annealing, (2) cyclic warm-restart schedules, and (3) loss-adaptive scheduling where τ responds to gradient signal magnitude. We also investigate per-head vs. global temperature parameters, and whether temperature itself can be made learnable via meta-gradients.

Experiments: Train 1.7B dense models on 500B tokens with various temperature schedules, comparing against fixed-gate baselines from the anchor paper. Evaluate on standard language modeling benchmarks, long-context tasks (RULER, Needle-in-Haystack), and attention sink metrics. Ablate scheduling strategies, head-level granularity, and interaction with learning rate schedules to disentangle curriculum effects from pure gating benefits.

title: Adaptive Gate Calibration for Cross-Lingual Transfer: Leveraging Sparse Attention Gates to Diagnose and Mitigate Language Imbalance in Multilingual LLMs
description: Problem: Multilingual LLMs trained on imbalanced corpora exhibit degraded performance on low-resource languages, partly because attention sinks concentrate disproportionately on high-resource language tokens during cross-lingual transfer. Existing mitigation strategies operate at the data or embedding level, ignoring the structural role of attention dynamics. Proposed Method: Building on the finding that head-specific sigmoid gates reduce attention sinks and induce query-dependent sparsity, we hypothesize that gated attention heads act as natural language-routing mechanisms. We propose Language-Adaptive Gate Calibration (LAGC), which (1) freezes a pretrained multilingual backbone and learns lightweight per-language gate scaling vectors appended to the sigmoid gate output, and (2) introduces a cross-lingual gate alignment loss that encourages low-resource languages to produce gate activation distributions similar to high-resource counterparts at matched semantic positions. We further use gate activation entropy as a diagnostic probe to quantify language-specific attention sink severity. Experiments: We train 1.7B dense models with gated attention on mC4 (covering 50 languages with controlled imbalance ratios), then fine-tune with LAGC. Evaluations cover XNLI, XQuAD, and FLORES-200 translation, comparing against mT5, language-specific adapters, and standard gated attention. Ablations isolate the gate alignment loss and per-language scaling contributions.

title: Adaptive Gating Frequency Across Transformer Layers: When and Where Does Sigmoid Gating Matter Most?
description:
Problem: The anchor paper applies head-specific sigmoid gating uniformly across all attention layers, but transformer layers are known to serve heterogeneous roles (early layers handle local syntax, middle layers semantic composition, late layers task-specific reasoning). Uniformly applying gating may be suboptimal—some layers may benefit greatly while others may experience interference or wasted capacity.

Proposed Method: We introduce Layer-Adaptive Gated Attention (LAGA), which learns a per-layer gating budget via differentiable sparsity penalties during training. Concretely, we parameterize each layer with a scalar 'gating temperature' that interpolates between ungated softmax attention and full sigmoid-gated attention. We additionally explore three structured schedules (early-heavy, late-heavy, alternating) against the learned adaptive assignment. We analyze which layers activate gating most strongly and correlate this with probing-based layer function analysis.

Experiments: (1) Train 1.7B dense models on 300B tokens under uniform vs. adaptive gating schedules; (2) Evaluate perplexity, downstream benchmarks (MMLU, HellaSwag, GSM8K), and long-context tasks (SCROLLS, RULER); (3) Ablate the effect of fixing gating to only top-k layers identified by LAGA; (4) Measure attention sink prevalence per layer as a function of gating assignment. We expect LAGA to outperform uniform gating with fewer gated layers, identifying a sparse critical set of layers where gating yields maximum benefit.

title: Adaptive Gate Initialization for Continual Pre-training: Leveraging Gated Attention to Mitigate Catastrophic Forgetting in Domain Adaptation
description:
Problem: When continually pre-training large language models on new domain-specific corpora (e.g., biomedical, legal, code), models suffer catastrophic forgetting of general capabilities. Existing mitigation strategies (replay, EWC, LoRA) add overhead or insufficiently preserve prior knowledge. Gated attention's head-specific sigmoid gates provide a natural, lightweight mechanism to selectively modulate which attention heads activate for new versus old knowledge, but this property has not been exploited for continual learning.

Proposed Method: We introduce GateShield, which initializes head-specific sigmoid gates from a pretrained gated-attention model, then during continual pre-training applies a gate-sparsity regularizer that penalizes deviation of gate activation distributions from their pretrained baseline. Gates that were highly sparse (near-zero) in the original model are constrained more tightly, preserving attention sinks-free behavior on general tasks. A small set of gates are selectively unfrozen via gradient-magnitude-based selection to absorb new domain knowledge.

Planned Experiments: (1) Continual pre-training of 1.7B gated vs. standard attention models on biomedical and code corpora; (2) Evaluate forgetting via MMLU, HellaSwag, and domain benchmarks (MedQA, HumanEval); (3) Ablate gate regularization strength, selection ratio, and compare against EWC, replay, and LoRA baselines; (4) Analyze gate activation shifts across domains to validate selectivity hypothesis.

title: Adaptive Gate Calibration for Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Reducing Distraction Sinks in Long-Context RAG Systems
description:
Problem: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems suffer from 'distraction' phenomena where irrelevant retrieved passages hijack attention patterns, analogous to attention sinks but driven by spurious high-frequency tokens in retrieved context rather than positional artifacts. Standard softmax attention amplifies this by concentrating probability mass on distractors. The gated attention finding—that head-specific sigmoid gates post-SDPA reduce attention sinks and improve long-context extrapolation—motivates a targeted solution for RAG.

Proposed Method: We introduce RAG-GateAttention, which augments gated attention with a retrieval-aware gate calibration mechanism. Specifically, we learn lightweight per-head gate bias terms conditioned on a binary relevance signal (derived from a small cross-encoder reranker score) that dynamically suppress gates for heads attending to low-relevance retrieved segments. During training, we use a contrastive objective pairing relevant/irrelevant retrieved documents to shape gate distributions. This requires no architecture changes beyond the sigmoid gate from the anchor paper.

Experiments: (1) Benchmark on MDQA, NaturalQuestions-RAG, and FRAMES with varying distractor counts (1–20 passages). (2) Ablations comparing standard softmax, vanilla gated attention, and RAG-GateAttention. (3) Attention visualization showing distraction-sink suppression. (4) Scaling study at 1.7B and 7B parameter ranges. (5) Long-context extrapolation on 32K–128K inputs with mixed relevant/irrelevant chunks.

title: Adaptive Gating Schedules for Attention: Learning When to Be Sparse During Training
description: Problem: The anchor paper demonstrates that a fixed sigmoid gate after SDPA improves performance and reduces attention sinks, but uses a static gating mechanism throughout training. We hypothesize that the optimal sparsity profile of attention gates should evolve during training—early stages may benefit from denser attention for broad pattern acquisition, while later stages benefit from sparser, more specialized gates. Proposed Method: We introduce Curriculum Gating, where the sigmoid gate's temperature parameter is scheduled during training. Specifically, we parameterize the gate as σ(g/τ(t)) where τ(t) is a learnable or scheduled temperature that anneals from high (near-uniform) to low (sparse) values over training steps. We also explore meta-learned per-layer gating schedules that adapt based on gradient signal magnitude and loss curvature, allowing layers to autonomously determine their sparsity trajectory. Experiments: We train 1.7B dense models on a 300B token subset, comparing (1) fixed gates (baseline from anchor), (2) linear temperature annealing, (3) cosine annealing, (4) meta-learned schedules, and (5) layer-wise adaptive schedules. We evaluate perplexity, attention sink formation dynamics via attention entropy curves during training, long-context extrapolation on SCROLLS/RULER benchmarks, and training stability under varying learning rates.

title: Adaptive Gate Calibration for Continual Learning in LLMs: Leveraging Sigmoid-Gated Attention to Mitigate Catastrophic Forgetting
description: Problem: Catastrophic forgetting remains a critical challenge when continually fine-tuning large language models on sequential task streams. Standard softmax attention tends to overwrite previously learned representations, while attention sinks concentrate information in fixed token positions, amplifying forgetting. We hypothesize that the sparse, query-dependent gating properties of sigmoid-gated attention (as identified in the anchor paper) can naturally protect consolidated knowledge by selectively routing gradients and reducing destructive interference during continual updates. Method: We propose GateCL, which freezes base model weights and instead learns task-specific gate scaling factors (low-rank modulations of the sigmoid gate magnitudes) for each new task. During forward passes, gates from previous tasks are regularized via an elastic-weight-consolidation-style penalty on gate activations rather than all parameters, exploiting the sparsity of gate scores to identify and protect task-critical attention heads. A lightweight gate-routing module selects relevant gate configurations at inference. Experiments: We evaluate on standard continual learning benchmarks (Split-CIFAR adapted to NLP, SuperGLUE sequential fine-tuning, domain-incremental language modeling) comparing against EWC, LoRA-based CL, and O-LoRA baselines. Ablations study gate sparsity levels, regularization strength, and whether attention-sink mitigation correlates with reduced forgetting across tasks and context lengths up to 32K tokens.

title: Adaptive Gate Calibration for Continual Learning in LLMs: Leveraging Sparse Gating to Mitigate Catastrophic Forgetting
description:
Problem: Continual learning in large language models suffers from catastrophic forgetting when fine-tuned on new tasks. Existing approaches (EWC, LoRA-based methods) either impose heavy computational overhead or fail to preserve prior task representations. The sparse gating mechanism from gated attention—which selectively modulates SDPA outputs in a query-dependent manner—offers an untapped opportunity: gates can act as lightweight, task-specific modulators without altering core attention weights.

Proposed Method: We introduce GateCL, which freezes pre-trained transformer weights and learns task-specific sigmoid gate parameters (head-specific, low-parameter overhead) for each new task. During continual learning, only gate vectors are updated, while shared attention parameters remain fixed. We further propose a gate consolidation regularizer that penalizes deviation from a reference gate distribution derived from prior tasks, preventing gate drift. For inference on mixed tasks, we introduce a lightweight task-router that selects appropriate gate configurations.

Experiments: (1) Benchmark on standard continual learning suites (Split-CIFAR adapted for text, SuperGLUE sequential tasks, code+math sequential fine-tuning). (2) Compare against EWC, PackNet, O-LoRA, and full fine-tuning baselines. (3) Ablate gate consolidation strength, number of tasks (up to 10), and model scale (1.7B to 7B). (4) Analyze gate sparsity patterns across tasks to understand specialization.

title: Adaptive Gate Calibration for Cross-Layer Attention Sink Redistribution in Long-Context LLMs
description: Problem: While head-specific sigmoid gating after SDPA mitigates attention sinks locally within each layer, attention sink patterns interact across layers in complex ways during long-context processing. Sinks suppressed in early layers may re-emerge or shift to later layers, leaving the full cross-layer dynamics unexplored and potentially suboptimal for very long sequences (>128K tokens). Proposed Method: We introduce Cross-Layer Gate Calibration (CLGC), where gate parameters are not learned independently per head but are conditioned on a lightweight cross-layer sink-density signal. Specifically, we maintain a running exponential moving average of per-head attention entropy across layers, and use this signal to modulate each head's gate initialization and learning rate schedule via a small auxiliary MLP. This creates a soft coordination mechanism that actively redistributes sink behavior across the network depth. During inference, we further propose a dynamic gate rescaling pass triggered when sink concentration exceeds a threshold, requiring no retraining. Experiments: (1) Pre-train 1.7B dense models on 500B tokens comparing baseline sigmoid gating vs. CLGC; (2) Evaluate perplexity on 32K/128K/256K context benchmarks (SCROLLS, Long-Range Arena, Needle-in-Haystack); (3) Measure attention entropy distributions across all layers; (4) Ablate cross-layer conditioning granularity and EMA decay rates. We expect CLGC to improve long-context extrapolation by 15-20% over per-head independent gating.

title: Adaptive Gating Frequency: Learning When to Gate Across Layers and Heads for Efficient Long-Context LLMs
description: Problem: While post-SDPA sigmoid gating uniformly improves attention across all layers and heads, different layers in transformers serve distinct roles (early layers handle local syntax, later layers handle long-range semantics). Applying the same gating mechanism uniformly may be suboptimal—some layers/heads may benefit more from sparse gating than others, and unnecessary gating could introduce computational overhead at inference time. Proposed Method: We introduce 'Selective Gated Attention' (SGA), which learns a per-layer, per-head binary gating decision (whether to apply sigmoid gating at all) through differentiable architecture search during training. A lightweight meta-controller predicts gating utility scores based on layer depth, head index, and sequence statistics, trained jointly with the LLM via a sparsity-encouraging regularization loss. This produces a heterogeneous gating pattern where only high-utility layer-head combinations receive sigmoid gates. Experiments: (1) Train 1.7B dense models on 500B tokens with uniform gating vs. SGA, comparing perplexity and downstream benchmarks; (2) Analyze learned gating patterns across layers/heads and correlate with attention entropy and sink behavior; (3) Evaluate long-context extrapolation (8K→32K) to assess whether selective gating better targets layers responsible for attention sinks; (4) Measure inference FLOPs reduction from sparsified gating patterns.

title: Adaptive Gate Calibration for Heterogeneous Attention Heads: Learning When to Gate and When Not To
description: Problem: The anchor paper applies a uniform head-specific sigmoid gate after SDPA across all layers and heads, but different attention heads serve distinct functional roles (e.g., induction heads, positional heads, semantic heads). Applying the same gating paradigm uniformly may over-regularize heads that benefit from dense, unsparse attention patterns, while under-regularizing others. We hypothesize that a meta-learned, layer-and-head-conditional gating policy can improve upon static sigmoid gating. Proposed Method: We introduce 'GateRouter,' a lightweight auxiliary network that takes as input head-level statistics (entropy of attention distribution, average attention sink mass, layer depth, token position) and outputs a continuous interpolation coefficient determining how much gating to apply per head per forward pass. GateRouter is jointly trained with the base model using a sparsity-aware auxiliary loss that encourages gating only when attention entropy exceeds a learned threshold. This allows certain heads to remain fully dense while others become sparse. Experiments: (1) Train 1.7B dense models on 100B tokens comparing uniform sigmoid gate vs. GateRouter; (2) Analyze per-head gate utilization patterns across layers; (3) Evaluate long-context extrapolation on SCROLLS and RULER benchmarks; (4) Ablate auxiliary loss weight and threshold initialization; (5) Measure training stability under varying learning rates.

title: Adaptive Gate Annealing: Dynamic Sparsity Scheduling in Gated Attention for Curriculum-Aware Long-Context Learning
description: Problem: While head-specific sigmoid gating after SDPA mitigates attention sinks and improves long-context extrapolation, the gating mechanism applies uniform sparsity pressure throughout training, ignoring the curriculum-like progression from short to long contexts and early vs. late training dynamics. We hypothesize that dynamically scheduling gate sparsity—starting dense (near-linear gating) and annealing toward sparser regimes—can accelerate early representation learning while achieving stronger long-context generalization at convergence. Method: We introduce Gate Annealing Schedules (GAS), where each head's sigmoid gate incorporates a learnable temperature parameter β(t) that is scheduled (cosine, linear, or learned via meta-gradient) across training steps. Early training uses high temperature (smooth, near-uniform gates), gradually cooling to induce sparsity. We additionally propose a context-length-conditional gate temperature that increases sparsity pressure proportionally to sequence length during training. This is implemented as a lightweight modification atop the established head-specific sigmoid gate. Experiments: We train 1.7B dense models on 300B tokens with varying annealing schedules, comparing against fixed-gate baselines and no-gate softmax attention. Evaluations include standard language modeling perplexity, long-context benchmarks (RULER, LongBench), attention sink diagnostics, and out-of-distribution length generalization (training at 4K, evaluating at 32K). Ablations isolate schedule type, meta-learned vs. fixed annealing, and per-head vs. global temperature.
